entries.ipa: /ɪn ədˈvæns əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ədˈvæn sə/
entries.register: formal to neutral; scheduling, logistics, and news writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in advance of filing). Never a that-clause. A nominal wh-clause is barely possible in sense 1 but is entirely normal in sense 2 (well in advance of what anyone expected).
entries.pattern: [clause] in advance of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · In advance of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Before plus foresight — it says not merely that one thing preceded another but that the earlier thing was done in preparation for the later one, which is why it collocates with deadlines, storms, votes, and deliveries. Against bare before, it is longer and adds that implication of deliberateness; against prior to, which adds nothing at all, it at least earns the extra words. Against ahead of, it is the more formal of the two and lacks ahead of's competitive sense 3. Bare in advance is an adverbial and takes no object: Pay in advance, Let me know in advance — where the preposition always needs one.
entries.meaning: 1. Earlier than, and in preparation for. The county opened shelters in advance of the storm. 2. Further developed than; ahead of (a standard or era). The design was years in advance of anything else on the market.
examples: The county opened four shelters in advance of the storm.
Ballots must be requested in advance of the October 20 deadline.
In advance of the vote, both sides released their whip counts.
She read the entire file in advance of meeting the family.
Payment is required in advance of delivery, not on receipt.
The design was years in advance of anything else on the market.
His thinking on the subject was well in advance of the profession's.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ænˌtɪsəˈpeɪʃən əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ænˌtɪsəˈpeɪʃə nə/
entries.register: formal to neutral; news writing, business, and scheduling
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in anticipation of moving abroad). Never a that-clause — the bare noun anticipation can take one (the anticipation that prices would fall), but the frozen preposition cannot, and anticipating that or plain expecting is how to write a clause. A free relative is fine (in anticipation of what the exhibit would draw).
entries.pattern: [clause] in anticipation of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · In anticipation of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Against in advance of, which treats the later event as settled fact, in anticipation of puts the reason inside the actor's head: the expected thing may never arrive, and the sentence is still true. That is the whole difference between shelters opened in advance of the storm (the storm came) and shelters opened in anticipation of a storm (they expected one). Against ahead of, it is the more explicitly motivated of the two. Bare in anticipation is an adverbial and takes no object: She waited in anticipation — where the preposition always needs one.
entries.meaning: Names the expected event that explains a preparation. Because the motive is an expectation rather than a fact, the phrase survives intact even when the anticipated thing never happens.
examples: The city stockpiled salt in anticipation of a hard winter.
In anticipation of the ruling, both firms had statements drafted.
Shares rose in anticipation of strong holiday sales.
She sold the second car in anticipation of moving abroad.
In anticipation of heavy turnout, the county added six machines.
The museum extended its hours in anticipation of what the exhibit would draw.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈkeɪs əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈkeɪs ə/
entries.register: neutral, with a strong pull toward signage and instructions
entries.complement: noun phrase only, and characteristically a bare article-less noun (in case of fire). Never a that-clause and never a wh-clause — for a clause you need the conjunction in case (Take an umbrella in case it rains) or in the event that.
entries.pattern: In case of [noun phrase], [imperative or clause]. · [clause] in case of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: In case of + noun phrase names the emergency; in case + clause names a precaution. In case of fire, use the stairs tells you what to do when there is a fire; Bring a flashlight in case the power goes out tells you to prepare for one. Substituting one for the other is the single most common error with this phrase.
entries.meaning: Names the situation that would trigger the instruction attached to it. It is the fixed formula of public safety notices and contract clauses, which is why it survives with a bare noun where ordinary English would demand an article.
examples: In case of fire, use the stairs.
In case of emergency, break the glass.
In case of a tie, the chair casts the deciding vote.
The policy explains what happens in case of cancellation.
In case of rain, the ceremony moves indoors.
Passengers should remain seated in case of turbulence.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈtʃɑrdʒ əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈtʃɑrdʒ ə/
entries.respell: in CHARJ uhv — the of reduces to a bare schwa, so in charge of it comes out in CHARJ uh-vit
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in charge of hiring), or a nominal wh-clause (in charge of what goes into the report). Never a that-clause. Frequently stranded or used with no complement at all, in which case of drops: Who's in charge here?
entries.pattern: [person] is in charge of [noun phrase] · the [person] in charge of [noun phrase] · [person] put someone in charge of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In charge of and in the charge of reverse the roles. The nurse in charge of the ward runs the ward; the ward in the charge of the nurse is the thing being run. The single word the flips who has the authority, and this is a genuine trap in formal writing.
entries.meaning: Assigns responsibility and authority over what follows. The noun charge here is the old sense "a duty entrusted to someone," now surviving almost nowhere else, which is what makes the phrase frozen: you cannot say in a charge of or in full charge of and keep the same meaning.
examples: She is in charge of the entire western region.
Who was in charge of locking up last night?
They put a twenty-six-year-old in charge of a hundred-million-dollar budget.
The agent in charge of the investigation refused to comment.
He is in charge of nothing and complains about everything.
I want to speak to whoever is in charge of customer accounts.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈdeɪndʒər əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈdeɪndʒə rə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund, and the gerund is much the commoner (in danger of losing the house, in danger of collapse). Because of is a preposition, in danger of to lose the house is wrong, and so is in danger to fall. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: be in danger of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · [noun] in danger of [verb-ing] · in real/serious/imminent danger of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: The bad outcome named after of is one the subject would suffer or commit, which is what keeps The bridge is in danger of collapsing right and The bridge is in danger of the flood wrong — the flood is the threat, not the outcome. For the threat itself the phrase is in danger from (in danger from rising water). Against at risk of, which takes identical complements, this is the more vivid and less statistical of the two; against on the verge of, which is neutral about whether the outcome is welcome, in danger of is always unwelcome. Bare in danger takes no object: She knew she was in danger.
entries.meaning: States a bad outcome the subject may be about to suffer or cause. It is one of the few members of this family whose default complement is a gerund rather than a noun, and it takes a degree adverb inside it — in real danger of, in serious danger of — the way in need of does.
examples: Two of the schools are in danger of losing accreditation.
The seawall is in danger of collapse within the decade.
He was in danger of missing the filing deadline entirely.
Nobody here is in any danger of being overpaid.
The species is in danger of disappearing from the state altogether.
She was in real danger of talking herself out of the job.

entries.ipa: /ɪn dɪˈfaɪəns əv/ · connected speech /ɪn dɪˈfaɪən sə/
entries.register: formal to neutral; news writing and legal reporting
entries.complement: noun phrase — an order, ban, law, or authority — or a gerund (in defiance of being told twice), or a free relative (in defiance of what the court had ordered). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in defiance of [noun phrase]. · In defiance of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: The deliberate twin of in violation of. In violation of reports that a rule was broken and says nothing about intent; in defiance of asserts that the breach was open and meant as a challenge, which is why it attaches to orders, bans, sanctions, and warnings rather than to section numbers. Against in spite of and despite, which merely concede an obstacle, this one requires an authority that was deliberately refused. It always carries a judgment — admiration or condemnation, depending on who is telling the story.
entries.meaning: Reports that the action was taken in open refusal of an authority. Because the phrase asserts intent, it is the wrong word wherever the actor may simply not have known the rule.
examples: The march went ahead in defiance of the mayor's order.
Three ships sailed in defiance of the blockade.
In defiance of the ban, the paper published the transcript in full.
She kept the clinic open in defiance of two cease-and-desist letters.
The council raised the levy in defiance of what the state auditor had recommended.
He stayed on the ballot in defiance of his own party's leadership.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ɪkˈsɛs əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ɪkˈsɛ sə/
entries.respell: in ik-SESS uhv — the noun here is /ɪkˈsɛs/, stressed on the second syllable, not the /ˈɛksɛs/ of excess baggage
entries.complement: a quantity expression only — a number, a sum, a measure, or a noun naming a limit (in excess of $2 million, in excess of the posted speed). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [quantity or clause] in excess of [quantity] · be in excess of [quantity] · amounts in excess of [figure]
entries.contrast: A four-word more than, and outside drafting more than is better: damages in excess of $50,000 is damages over $50,000. It earns its length only where the threshold is legally operative, which is why it is the standard phrasing of jurisdictional minimums, coverage caps, and permit limits. Against over, it has the advantage of being unmistakable — over $50,000 can be misread as spatial or temporal in a crowded sentence, and in excess of cannot. Against short of, it is the exact opposite: one passes the line, the other stops before it.
entries.meaning: States that a figure passes a stated threshold. It is a threshold word rather than a comparison word: the object has to be a limit, not simply another quantity being ranked against it.
examples: The plaintiff seeks damages in excess of $75,000.
Repairs are expected to run in excess of two million dollars.
Loads in excess of four tons require a permit.
The fund has held cash in excess of its stated target for six quarters.
Any hours in excess of forty are paid at time and a half.
Rainfall was in excess of the seasonal average for the third year running.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in favor of raising the cap), or a nominal wh-clause (in favor of whatever gets the building open). Never a that-clause — for that you need in favor of the proposition that. The predicative pattern be in favor of is the commonest form.
entries.pattern: be in favor of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · [reject/drop X] in favor of [noun phrase] · rule/decide in favor of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against for, this is the deliberative register — I'm for it in conversation, I am in favor of the amendment in a meeting. Against instead of, sense 2 adds a note of preference and judgment: you drop one thing in favor of a better one, but you simply do one thing instead of another. Bare in favor is not this preposition — with no complement it is an adverbial phrase meaning "supporting the motion" (Three voted in favor, two against), and the possessive in his favor is a different construction again (The ruling went in his favor).
variants: in favour of is the British spelling
American English uses favor without the u.
entries.meaning: 1. Supporting. Nine members voted in favor of the measure. 2. Choosing one thing over another. The city dropped the streetcar plan in favor of dedicated bus lanes. 3. To the legal or financial advantage of. The court ruled in favor of the tenants.
examples: Nine members voted in favor of the measure.
Are you in favor of moving the meeting to Thursday?
The city dropped the streetcar plan in favor of dedicated bus lanes.
She turned down the corporate offer in favor of a research fellowship.
The court ruled in favor of the tenants.
Write the check in favor of the trust, not the individual.
Public opinion has shifted sharply in favor of the proposal.

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun (in front of me, never in front of I). No gerund — in front of leaving is impossible, because the object has to be a thing or a person that occupies space. Never a that-clause. A free relative is fine when it names such a thing (in front of what used to be the courthouse), since a free relative is a noun phrase; a wh-clause that names a proposition is not (in front of whether he agreed is nonsense).
entries.pattern: [clause] in front of [noun phrase] · In front of [noun phrase], [clause]. · right/directly/just in front of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In front of and in the front of are different prepositions. In front of the bus is outside it, ahead of it; in the front of the bus is inside it, in the forward section. Against before, in front of is the ordinary spatial word — before in a spatial sense is formal or literary (He knelt before the altar). Against opposite and across from, in front of does not require the two things to face each other. Bare in front is an adverb, not this preposition, and takes no object: the car in front and He sat in front are complete, where in front of demands one — the car in front of us.
entries.meaning: 1. Positioned ahead of something, facing it or blocking it. A truck was parked in front of the hydrant. 2. In the presence of an audience, especially an inhibiting one. Don't say that in front of the children.
examples: A truck was parked in front of the hydrant.
Meet me in front of the library at six.
She spilled the whole cup right in front of him.
Don't say that in front of the children.
He had to defend the budget in front of the entire board.
There were forty people in front of us in line.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈlu əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈlu ə/
entries.respell: in LOO uhv (British English often /ɪn ˈljuː əv/, in LYOO uhv)
entries.register: formal; legal, financial, and funeral-notice English
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in lieu of paying cash); a nominal wh-clause is possible but formal (in lieu of what was promised). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in lieu of [noun phrase] · In lieu of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Semantically identical to instead of and in place of, but three registers higher. In lieu of belongs in wills, leases, and obituaries; using it in casual speech reads as stiff or as a mistake for in view of, which it is often confused with and which means something completely different ("considering").
entries.meaning: Substitutes one thing for another that was expected or owed. Lieu is a fossil — a French word for "place" that survives in English in this phrase and essentially nowhere else — so the expression admits no modification at all.
examples: In lieu of flowers, the family asks for donations to the food bank.
He accepted stock in lieu of a year-end bonus.
The company offered store credit in lieu of a refund.
Employees may take compensatory time in lieu of overtime pay.
The tenant paid two months' rent in lieu of notice.
In lieu of a formal hearing, the parties agreed to arbitration.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈlaɪt əv/ · flapped /ɪn ˈlaɪɾ əv/ · casual /ɪn ˈlaɪɾ ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in light of what we learned yesterday). Never a that-clause — write in light of the fact that if you need one.
entries.pattern: In light of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in light of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Near-identical to in view of and given, but in light of implies new information that reframes what came before — you reconsider something in light of fresh evidence. In view of is neutral about novelty. Do not confuse with in lieu of, which means "instead of."
variants: in the light of is the dominant British form
American English overwhelmingly drops the article.
entries.meaning: Introduces the consideration that explains or justifies the decision in the main clause. The metaphor is illumination: the object shines on the situation and changes how it looks.
examples: In light of the new evidence, the charges were dropped.
The board reconsidered the layoffs in light of record third-quarter earnings.
In light of recent events, the reception has been postponed.
Her comments look very different in light of what we learned yesterday.
In light of his age, the judge suspended the sentence.
The guidance was rewritten in light of the audit findings.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈnid əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈni də/
entries.complement: noun phrase, very often an abstract bare noun (in need of repair). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, and never an infinitive — in need of to rest is impossible, and even the gerund is awkward: in need of rest, not in need of resting.
entries.pattern: be in need of [noun phrase] · [noun] in need of [noun phrase] · badly/urgently/sorely in need of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In need of is the adjectival, describing form; plain need is the verb. The roof needs repair and the roof is in need of repair mean the same thing, but the phrase is more formal and, unlike the verb, can modify a noun directly: a roof in need of repair.
entries.meaning: States a deficiency as a property of the subject. This is one of the few complex prepositions that accepts a degree adverb inside it — badly in need of, sorely in need of — because need here retains enough of its nominal life to be measured.
examples: The building is in need of serious structural work.
He arrived tired, hungry, and in need of a shower.
Families in need of assistance should call the county office.
The argument is sound but badly in need of editing.
She is in need of nothing so much as a week off.
This is a neighborhood in need of investment, not surveillance.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in place of what was there before). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in place of [noun phrase] · In place of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with instead of in most contexts, but in place of keeps a stronger sense of physical or structural substitution — one thing occupying the slot the other vacated. Instead of is the everyday word and the only one of the three that comfortably takes a gerund in speech; in lieu of is the formal one. Do not confuse with the literal string in the place of, which means "in that location."
entries.meaning: Marks a replacement filling a role. The substitute and the original are understood to be comparable — same job, different filler.
examples: Use olive oil in place of butter.
The deputy chaired the meeting in place of the director.
In place of the annual review, managers will hold quarterly check-ins.
They planted native grasses in place of the lawn.
A photograph hung in place of the mirror that had broken.
He offered an apology in place of an explanation.

entries.ipa: /ɪn rɪˈsit əv/ · connected speech /ɪn rɪˈsi də/
entries.respell: in ruh-SEET uhv (the p is silent)
entries.complement: noun phrase; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative is possible but stiff and rare (in receipt of what the court had ordered).
entries.pattern: be in receipt of [noun phrase] · upon being in receipt of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: A four-word way of saying have received, and almost always worse. We are in receipt of your letter says exactly what We received your letter says, at twice the length. Keep it only where a formal record is genuinely wanted — benefit determinations, acknowledgments of legal service.
entries.meaning: Marks the subject as having taken delivery of something. It survives almost entirely in fixed openings of business letters and in social-services language (households in receipt of benefits).
examples: We are in receipt of your letter of March 3.
Households in receipt of federal assistance are exempt from the fee.
The clerk confirmed that the office was in receipt of the filing.
Once in receipt of payment, we will release the shipment.
Any employee in receipt of such a notice should contact HR immediately.

entries.ipa: /ɪn rɪˈspɛkt əv/ · connected speech /ɪn rɪˈspɛk tə/
entries.register: formal; British and legal. Flagged: this is not the ordinary American form.
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in respect of what was paid). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in respect of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In respect of means "concerning, with regard to" — it has nothing to do with admiration. American editors will usually change it to with respect to, regarding, or plain about or for. Note that with respect to is neutral and standard in American usage while in respect of reads as an importation.
variants: in respect to is a chiefly American variant, itself less common than with respect to, which is the form American writers actually use. British and Commonwealth legal drafting prefers in respect of.
entries.meaning: Introduces the matter the statement is limited to. In British legal and accounting prose it is the default way to attach a topic to a claim; in American prose it is a marked, faintly foreign choice.
examples: No claim may be brought in respect of losses arising before the policy date.
The company made provision in respect of deferred tax.
Payments in respect of prior years must be listed separately.
She was questioned in respect of three separate incidents.
Nothing is owed in respect of the canceled order.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈsɜrtʃ əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈsɜrtʃ ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, and never a gerund, since what is sought must be a thing (in search of work, not in search of working). Never a that-clause. A free relative naming a thing is fine and is common (in search of whatever work they could find, in search of what was left of the wreck).
entries.pattern: [clause] in search of [noun phrase] · In search of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: In search of states a purpose and implies motion or effort; looking for is the plain equivalent. Compare in need of, which states a lack without implying that anyone is doing anything about it.
entries.meaning: Names what a journey or effort is aimed at obtaining. Almost always follows a verb of motion or of striving, and it is the standard headline formula for a quest.
examples: They moved north in search of work.
He spent the afternoon in search of a parking space.
Whales travel thousands of miles in search of food.
In search of quiet, she rented a cabin for the winter.
Reporters descended on the town in search of a story.
The expedition set out in search of the wreck.
They spent two seasons in search of whatever the first party had left behind.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈspaɪt əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈspaɪ də/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in spite of being warned). Never a that-clause — in spite of that he was warned is impossible, and for a clause you must write in spite of the fact that or switch to the conjunction although. A nominal wh-clause is marginal here and best avoided.
entries.pattern: In spite of [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause]. · [clause] in spite of [noun phrase / verb-ing].
entries.contrast: Fully interchangeable with despite, which has exactly the same complement rule: despite takes a noun phrase (despite the forecast) or a gerund (despite being warned) and never a that-clause — despite that he was warned is wrong, and despite the fact that he was warned is the workaround. Despite is one word shorter and marginally more formal; the only real difference is length and rhythm. Two errors to avoid: the blend despite of, which is never correct in either direction, and in spite of that-clause. In spite of has no connection to the noun spite meaning malice — nobody is being spiteful.
entries.meaning: Concedes a fact that would ordinarily have prevented what the main clause reports. The concession and the outcome are both asserted as true, which distinguishes this from a conditional.
examples: In spite of the forecast, we went ahead with the picnic.
She finished the race in spite of a torn hamstring.
In spite of everything, the two of them stayed close.
The bridge held in spite of decades of deferred maintenance.
He signed the contract in spite of being warned by three lawyers.
In spite of its size, the truck handles like a sedan.

entries.ipa: /ɪn səˈpɔrt əv/ · connected speech /ɪn səˈpɔr də/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in support of raising the cap), or a free relative (in support of what the union had asked for). Never a that-clause — for a clause the drafting form is in support of the proposition that, and ordinary prose uses to support.
entries.pattern: [clause] in support of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · In support of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [evidence / testimony / a brief] in support of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against in favor of, which reports a position held, in support of reports an action taken to advance something: you are in favor of the bill, and you march, testify, or file a brief in support of it. Substituting one for the other turns an opinion into an act or an act into an opinion. Against plain for, it is the formal, active choice and is the fixed term of court filings (a brief in support of the motion). The literal engineering sense the phrase grew out of is still live — a beam in support of a floor.
entries.meaning: Names the cause an action is meant to advance. The complement is what benefits; the main clause supplies the effort.
examples: Thousands marched in support of the striking teachers.
She filed a brief in support of the plaintiffs.
In support of the application, the school submitted four years of test data.
He spoke in support of raising the cap on class size.
The company donated equipment in support of the cleanup.
Nothing in the record was offered in support of what the witness claimed.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈtɜrmz əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈtɜrmz ə/
entries.register: neutral in sense 1; sense 2 is criticized filler
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in terms of what we should do, in terms of how it is funded). Never a that-clause: in terms of what we should do is fine because what we should do is a noun-phrase equivalent, but in terms of that we should act is impossible.
entries.pattern: [clause] in terms of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · In terms of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is precise and useful; sense 2 is a vague topic marker that usually replaces a sharper preposition. Costs rose in terms of labor almost always means labor costs rose. Where in terms of can be swapped for about, for, as for, or nothing at all, cut it.
entries.meaning: 1. Measured in the units of; expressed by reference to. The budget is written in terms of constant 2019 dollars. 2. As regards (a vague topic marker). In terms of staffing, we're in decent shape.
examples: The budget is written in terms of constant 2019 dollars.
Thinking about distance in terms of travel time changes the map completely.
Explain the result in terms of the underlying chemistry.
In terms of staffing, we're in decent shape.
In terms of cost, the two proposals are indistinguishable.
She's improved a lot in terms of accuracy, less so in terms of speed.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ði ˈæbsəns əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ði ˈæbsəns ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause and never a wh-clause; never a gerund. The workaround for a clause is the conjunction unless or if there is no.
entries.pattern: In the absence of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in the absence of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: In the absence of means "when there is no X" and is a near-synonym of without and failing. Without is the everyday word; in the absence of is the drafting word and is preferred where the absence is a formally relevant condition. Do not confuse the frozen phrase with the literal in the absence of the chairman meaning "while the chairman is away," which is also idiomatic and uses the same words.
entries.meaning: Supplies the negative condition under which the main clause holds. It is the standard opening of default rules in statutes, contracts, and scientific reasoning.
examples: In the absence of evidence, the committee declined to act.
In the absence of a written agreement, state law governs.
Plants grown in the absence of light lose their color within days.
The vice chair presides in the absence of the chair.
In the absence of any objection, the motion carries.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈkeɪs əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ðə ˈkeɪ sə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative (in the case of what the auditors flagged). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: In the case of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in the case of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: In the case of and in case of are different prepositions, and the article is the whole difference. In case of fire names an emergency and attaches an instruction to it; in the case of the Hartford plant names one instance already under discussion and says something about it. The first is a contingency, the second an example — and In the case of fire, use the stairs is not idiomatic English. Against as for and with regard to, this one singles out one member of a set the reader already knows; against plain for, it is the longer form and is usually cuttable, since in the case of older buildings is normally just for older buildings.
entries.meaning: Singles out one instance from a set and restricts the statement to it. It presupposes that the set has already been established, which is why it so often follows a general claim rather than opening one.
examples: In the case of older buildings, the inspection is more thorough.
The rule is different in the case of part-time employees.
In the case of the Hartford plant, the layoffs began in March.
Refunds are automatic, except in the case of tickets bought through a reseller.
In the case of twins, the benefit is paid twice.
Nothing was done in the case of what the auditors flagged last spring.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈkɔrs əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ðə ˈkɔrs ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in the course of reviewing the file). Never a that-clause — the object has to name an activity, not a proposition, though a free relative that names one is fine (in the course of what turned into a four-hour meeting).
entries.pattern: In the course of [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause]. · [clause] in the course of [noun phrase / verb-ing].
entries.contrast: A formal during that adds the idea of an extended process rather than a mere span of time. During the meeting is neutral; in the course of the meeting implies things unfolded. The employment-law fixed phrase is in the course of employment, where no substitution is possible.
entries.meaning: Locates an event inside a longer activity, usually one that had its own momentum. Because course means a run or progression, the complement is nearly always an activity noun, not a point in time.
examples: In the course of the investigation, three more accounts surfaced.
She mentioned it only once in the course of a two-hour interview.
Injuries sustained in the course of employment are covered.
In the course of reviewing the file, the auditor found the discrepancy.
Languages change enormously in the course of a few centuries.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ði ɪˈvɛnt əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ði ɪˈvɛn də/
entries.complement: noun phrase only, and a gerund at a pinch (in the event of the tenant's defaulting). Never a that-clause — the clause-taking form is the conjunction in the event that (in the event that the flight is canceled), which is a different item.
entries.pattern: In the event of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in the event of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: In the event of and in case of both take a bare noun and both name a triggering situation; in case of is the shorter, more public-facing one (signs and instructions), while in the event of is the contract-drafting one. Neither takes a clause. Against if, both are nominal: if the flight is canceled versus in the event of cancellation.
entries.meaning: Names a contingency and attaches the rule that applies when it occurs. The pairing with in the event that is the cleanest illustration in the whole class of the noun-phrase-versus-clause split.
examples: In the event of cancellation, tickets will be refunded in full.
In the event of a power failure, the generators start automatically.
The lease terminates in the event of the tenant's death.
In the event of a dispute, the matter goes to arbitration.
Coverage continues in the event of a temporary layoff.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈfeɪs əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ðə ˈfeɪs ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically an abstract noun of difficulty (criticism, adversity, opposition); a gerund is possible but rare (in the face of being outvoted). Never a that-clause. A free relative is fine (in the face of what the auditors found).
entries.pattern: [clause] in the face of [noun phrase]. · In the face of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Frozen in the face of means "confronted with, and despite"; the literal string in the face of the cliff means an actual face or surface, and the two are told apart only by whether the complement is abstract. Against in spite of, this one insists that the obstacle was live and pressing at the time, not merely a background fact.
entries.meaning: Sets the main clause against active opposition or danger. It nearly always carries admiration or defiance, which is why it collocates so heavily with courage, stood firm, pressed on, and held.
examples: She kept her composure in the face of relentless questioning.
In the face of mounting evidence, the company finally issued a recall.
The crew stayed calm in the face of real danger.
He refused to resign in the face of enormous pressure.
In the face of a shrinking budget, the library extended its hours anyway.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈfɔrm əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ðə ˈfɔr mə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a gerund naming an activity (in the form of matching what employees give). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the form of [noun phrase]. · [abstract noun] in the form of [concrete noun]
entries.contrast: It specifies the shape a thing turned out to have, and its object must be a kind of the thing already named: help arrived in the form of a loan works because a loan is a kind of help, and the sentence collapses where that is not true (help arrived in the form of Tuesday). Against as, which does the same work in one word (arrived as a loan), the phrase is heavier but clearer when the two nouns are far apart in the sentence. Against such as, which offers one member of a class as an example, in the form of identifies the whole of the thing rather than a sample of it.
entries.meaning: Names the concrete shape an abstract thing took. The pattern is almost always abstract noun first, concrete noun second, and reversing it produces nonsense.
examples: Help arrived in the form of a state loan.
The bonus is paid in the form of stock, not cash.
Relief came in the form of three days of steady rain.
Opposition surfaced in the form of a petition with four thousand signatures.
The city offers support in the form of matching what residents raise themselves.
The evidence was circumstantial, mostly in the form of phone records.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ði ˈɪntrəst əv/ · also /ˈɪntərəst/ · connected speech /ɪn ði ˈɪntrə stə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in the interest of getting this finished). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: In the interest of [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause]. · [clause] in the interest of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Two readings that pull apart on the object. With an abstract value — time, clarity, fairness, safety — it names a goal being served, and it is very often a polite way of cutting something short: in the interest of time, let's move on. With a person or body it names a beneficiary, and there it competes with on behalf of, which claims an agency this phrase does not: a trustee acts on behalf of the estate and in the interest of the heirs. Against for the sake of, the two are close, but for the sake of leans toward people and in the interest of toward procedural values.
variants: The plural in the interests of is equally standard and is the commoner form in British English
American writers lean to the singular, and in the interest of time is fixed in the singular.
entries.meaning: Names the value or party the action is meant to serve. It presents the action as justified rather than merely explained, which is why it is standard in rulings, minutes, and public statements.
examples: In the interest of time, we'll take two more questions.
The names were withheld in the interest of privacy.
In the interest of fairness, both sides got the same twenty minutes.
The board acted in the interest of the shareholders, not the founders.
In the interest of getting this finished before June, I've cut the second phase.
The records were sealed in the interest of protecting the children involved.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈmɪdl̩ əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ðə ˈmɪdl̩ ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in the middle of eating), or a nominal wh-clause (in the middle of what he was saying). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the middle of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · In the middle of [noun phrase], [clause]. · right/smack in the middle of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Unlike most of this family, in the middle of is only half frozen: it takes intensifiers (right in the middle of, smack in the middle of) and it has a live literal reading. Against among and amid, it locates a point, not a scattering. Against during, sense 2 adds interruption — during dinner is neutral, in the middle of dinner means the dinner got broken into.
entries.meaning: 1. At or near the center of a space. There was a table in the middle of the room. 2. Partway through an activity, usually interrupted. He called me in the middle of dinner.
examples: There was a long table in the middle of the room.
The town sits right in the middle of the state.
They built the house smack in the middle of a hundred acres.
He called me in the middle of dinner.
I'm in the middle of something — can I call you back?
The power went out in the middle of the third quarter.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈmɪdst əv/ · casual /ɪn ðə ˈmɪs əv/ — the d routinely drops
entries.register: formal to neutral, with a literary tilt
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in the midst of moving). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the midst of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · In the midst of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Against in the middle of, which is the everyday word, in the midst of sits a register higher and takes a different kind of object: the middle of prefers a single bounded thing (the middle of the room, the middle of dinner), while the midst of prefers a plural, a mass, or an abstraction — in the midst of strangers, in the midst of a recession, in the midst of all that noise. It also lacks the interruption that in the middle of dinner carries: this phrase says "surrounded by," not "broken into." Against amid, it is the three-word equivalent and means the same thing. Bare midst is not a preposition in modern English; apart from this phrase it survives only in in our midst.
entries.meaning: Places the subject inside something extended and surrounding — a crowd, a crisis, a stretch of turbulent time. The object is nearly always plural, mass, or abstract.
examples: She stood in the midst of a crowd that would not move.
The company hired forty people in the midst of a hiring freeze everywhere else.
In the midst of the worst drought in decades, the district approved a golf course.
He resigned in the midst of an investigation he had asked for.
In the midst of all that noise, nobody heard the alarm.
They were in the midst of moving when the offer came through.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈneɪm əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ðə ˈneɪm ə/
entries.register: neutral to formal; sense 2 is rhetorical
entries.complement: noun phrase in sense 1; noun phrase or gerund in sense 2 (in the name of protecting the public, in the name of keeping costs down), which is where the phrase is most productive. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the name of [noun phrase] · In the name of [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause/imperative].
entries.contrast: Against on behalf of, which means "as the agent of" and is neutral, in the name of carries authority or invocation — you act on behalf of a client but in the name of the law. Sense 2 is almost always critical: things done in the name of progress are things the speaker doubts were progress. Note that only sense 2 takes the gerund — He signed in the name of the United States (sense 1) cannot become in the name of signing.
entries.meaning: 1. Using the authority of; invoking. Open up, in the name of the law. 2. Under the justification of (usually with an implication that the justification is false). Whole neighborhoods were leveled in the name of urban renewal.
examples: Open the door, in the name of the law.
The property is registered in the name of her late husband.
He signed the treaty in the name of the United States.
Whole neighborhoods were leveled in the name of urban renewal.
Terrible things have been done in the name of efficiency.
In the name of transparency, they released a document with half the pages blacked out.
The library cut its hours in the name of protecting the endowment.
In the name of keeping the peace, she said nothing for eleven years.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈprɑsɛs əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ðə ˈprɑsɛs ə/
entries.complement: gerund above all (in the process of moving), or a process noun (in the process of renovation). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, and never an infinitive — in the process of to move is wrong, and so is in the process to move.
entries.pattern: be in the process of [verb-ing] · [clause], and in the process of [verb-ing], [clause]
entries.contrast: Nearly always a wordier progressive: We are in the process of reviewing your application says what We are reviewing your application says. It survives because it signals that the process is long and the speaker is not finished — which is why it is the natural language of customer service and of construction schedules. Bare in the process is an adverbial, not this preposition: They rebuilt the engine and wrecked the transmission in the process has no object and cannot take one.
entries.meaning: Places the subject partway through an ongoing activity. It is the one member of the in the ___ of family whose default complement is a gerund rather than a noun.
examples: We are in the process of reviewing your application.
The company is in the process of relocating its headquarters.
She was in the process of changing careers when the offer came.
The building is in the process of renovation and will reopen in the fall.
They are still in the process of deciding whether to appeal.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈweɪk əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ðə ˈweɪ kə/
entries.register: formal; the standard idiom of news writing
entries.complement: noun phrase, almost always naming a disruptive event; a gerund is possible but uncommon (in the wake of losing the contract). Never a that-clause — the workaround is after + clause. A free relative naming the event is fine (in the wake of what happened in March).
entries.pattern: In the wake of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in the wake of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: More than after: it asserts consequence, not just sequence. After the hurricane is chronology; in the wake of the hurricane says the hurricane caused what follows. The metaphor is a ship's wake, so the complement should be something big enough to leave one — in the wake of lunch is a joke.
entries.meaning: Marks the aftermath of a major event as the cause or setting of the main clause. It combines the temporal work of after with the causal work of because of, which is exactly why journalists reach for it.
examples: In the wake of the recall, sales fell by a third.
Three executives resigned in the wake of the audit.
In the wake of the storm, half the county was without power.
New disclosure rules were adopted in the wake of the scandal.
In the wake of her departure, the department reorganized twice.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈvju əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˈvju ə/
entries.register: formal in sense 1; neutral in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause in sense 1 (in view of what happened last year). Never a that-clause — use in view of the fact that. Sense 2, the literal spatial one, takes a noun phrase only.
entries.pattern: In view of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in view of [noun phrase]. · be in view of [noun phrase] (literal)
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is a formal because of and a close synonym of in light of and given; sense 2 is the literal, spatial reading. Do not confuse with in lieu of ("instead of") — the two are frequently swapped by writers who half-remember the phrase, and the resulting sentence means the opposite of what was intended.
entries.meaning: 1. Considering; because of. In view of the delay, the fee has been waived. 2. Within sight of (literal). The cabin stands in view of the lake.
examples: In view of the delay, the registration fee has been waived.
The sentence was reduced in view of his cooperation.
In view of what happened last year, the policy seems reasonable.
The cabin stands in view of the lake.
They camped in view of the summit and waited for the weather to clear.
In view of rising costs, the district postponed the project.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˌvaɪəˈleɪʃən əv/ · connected speech /ɪn ˌvaɪəˈleɪʃə nə/
entries.register: formal; legal, regulatory, and news writing
entries.complement: noun phrase — a statute, rule, order, permit, or agreement — or a free relative standing in for one (in violation of what the order plainly required). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] in violation of [noun phrase] · [noun] in violation of [noun phrase] · be in violation of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The negative counterpart of in accordance with and pursuant to: those report that the action followed the rule, this alleges that it broke one. The object must be an instrument that could be named and cited — which is why the phrase is so often followed by a section number — and that is what separates it from contrary to, which covers mere advice and expectations: you act contrary to advice, but in violation of a statute. Against plain against, it is the formal, citable form. Milder alternatives that stop short of alleging a breach are inconsistent with and at variance with.
entries.meaning: Alleges that the action broke a specific rule that governed it. Because the claim is legally loaded, careful writers use it only where the instrument can be identified and the breach is being asserted, not merely suspected.
examples: The fence was built in violation of the setback ordinance.
Three trades were made in violation of the firm's own policy.
The court held that the search was in violation of the Fourth Amendment.
Dumping in violation of the permit carries a fine for each day it continues.
She was dismissed in violation of the collective bargaining agreement.
In violation of the cease-fire, shelling resumed before dawn.

entries.ipa: /ɪn əˈkɔrdəns wɪθ/ · also /wɪð/ before a vowel · weak /wəθ/, /wəð/
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (in accordance with what the permit requires). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] in accordance with [noun phrase]. · In accordance with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: In accordance to is always an error — the noun accordance takes with. Against according to, which reports what a source says, in accordance with reports conformity to a rule: According to the manual, the valve closes (the manual says so) versus The valve was installed in accordance with the manual (the installation followed it).
entries.meaning: States that the action conformed to a governing rule, standard, or instrument. It is the workhorse of compliance language and is almost never the right choice in ordinary prose, where under, following, or as required by will do.
examples: The audit was conducted in accordance with generally accepted standards.
Ballots will be counted in accordance with state law.
In accordance with your instructions, we have canceled the order.
The device must be installed in accordance with the manufacturer's specifications.
Benefits are calculated in accordance with the schedule in Appendix B.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in addition to running the shop), or a nominal wh-clause (in addition to what the grant covers). Never a that-clause and — because this to is a preposition, not an infinitive marker — never a bare infinitive: in addition to run the shop is wrong, and in addition to running the shop is the only correct form.
entries.pattern: In addition to [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause]. · [clause] in addition to [noun phrase / verb-ing].
entries.contrast: Verb agreement trap. In addition to does not create a compound subject: The manager, in addition to two clerks, was present — singular, because only the manager is the subject. Coordinating and would make it were. The same rule governs as well as, along with, and together with. Against besides, this is the fuller, more formal version; against plus, the more written one. Bare in addition is a conjunctive adverb, not this preposition, and takes no object: The fee covers materials. In addition, there is a lab charge.
entries.meaning: Adds a second item to what the main clause already says. The added material is presented as supplementary, which is why it does not count toward the subject.
examples: In addition to the tuition, students pay a lab fee.
She speaks Portuguese in addition to Spanish and French.
In addition to running the shop, he teaches two nights a week.
The senator, in addition to three staffers, was subpoenaed.
In addition to being cheaper, the new part is easier to install.
The package includes breakfast in addition to airport transfers.

entries.register: formal; institutional in sense 1, scientific in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in association with [noun phrase] · [noun] in association with [noun phrase] · presented in association with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Two lives, and the register tells them apart. In credit lines and event billing it is a politer, looser in conjunction with: institutions co-present things in association with each other, where machines and medicines are used in conjunction with each other. In research writing it is a deliberately weak causal word — in association with claims co-occurrence and nothing more, which is exactly why journals prefer it to caused by or because of. A reader who treats sense 2 as a causal claim has misread it, and a writer who uses it hoping the reader will is being slippery.
entries.meaning: 1. Jointly with; in partnership with. The festival is presented in association with the city arts commission. 2. Occurring together with; correlated with (technical, and expressly not causal). Elevated readings were observed in association with long-term use.
examples: The festival is presented in association with the city arts commission.
The report was produced in association with two university laboratories.
The exhibit travels in association with the national gallery.
In association with the merger, four executives took early retirement.
Elevated readings were observed in association with long-term use.
The rash appears in association with the second dose, not the first.
Fatigue was reported in association with several of the older drugs.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in comparison with what we paid last year). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in comparison with [noun phrase]. · In comparison with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A heavier compared with or than. Where a simple comparative will carry the sentence (This one is cheaper), the phrase is padding. Against relative to, which is neutral and quantitative, in comparison with is discursive. Bare in comparison is an adverbial, not this preposition: Last year was mild. This winter, in comparison, has been brutal.
variants: in comparison to is equally standard in American English
with is slightly preferred when the two things are being measured against each other, to when one is being likened to the other. Both are acceptable.
entries.meaning: Sets the main clause's subject beside a benchmark. Because it is bulky, it earns its place mainly when the benchmark is long or when the comparison needs to be fronted for emphasis.
examples: In comparison with last year, enrollment is up nine percent.
The salary looks generous in comparison with the regional average.
Our losses were trivial in comparison with theirs.
In comparison with the original, the remake feels weightless.
The drug performed well in comparison with the placebo.

entries.ipa: /ɪn kəmˈplaɪəns wɪθ/ · also /wɪð/ before a vowel · weak /wəθ/, /wəð/
entries.complement: noun phrase — a rule, order, permit, standard, or agreement — or a free relative standing in for one (in compliance with what the order required). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be in compliance with [noun phrase] · [clause] in compliance with [noun phrase]. · In compliance with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Three phrases worth learning as a set: in compliance with reports that a duty was met, in accordance with reports that a procedure was followed, and in violation of alleges that a rule was broken. In compliance with presupposes an obligation the subject was under and usually implies that somebody checks, which is why it belongs to inspections, audits, and consent decrees rather than to ordinary description. Against under, which is shorter and better in ordinary prose, it earns its length only where compliance itself is the thing being asserted.
variants: In compliance to is an error — the noun compliance takes with, exactly as accordance does. The negative is out of compliance with, the standard regulatory phrasing for a lapse that is being corrected rather than prosecuted.
entries.meaning: States that the subject has met an obligation imposed on it. The phrase is evaluative in a way in accordance with is not: somebody was required to do this, and did.
examples: The facility is now in compliance with federal emissions limits.
All three buildings were brought in compliance with the fire code.
Records are retained in compliance with the state's retention schedule.
In compliance with the court's order, the agency released the remaining pages.
Contractors must certify that their subcontractors are in compliance with the wage rules.
The district reported that it was in compliance with what the settlement required.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in conjunction with [noun phrase]. · In conjunction with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Means "jointly with" or "used together with," not merely "and." Against along with and together with, which just add an item, in conjunction with asserts that the two things operate together as a unit. Against in association with, it is the more mechanical of the two: things are used in conjunction with each other, institutions do things in association with each other.
entries.meaning: Marks joint operation or joint sponsorship. The two things named are doing something together, which is why the phrase is standard on instructions (use in conjunction with) and on event billing (presented in conjunction with).
examples: The exhibit was organized in conjunction with the state historical society.
This medication should not be taken in conjunction with alcohol.
In conjunction with the new sensors, the software can detect leaks earlier.
The training runs in conjunction with the annual conference.
Read this section in conjunction with the warranty terms on page 12.

entries.register: formal; legal, police, and corporate language
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in connection with filing the claim), or a free relative (in connection with what happened on the tenth). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in connection with [noun phrase]. · In connection with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A deliberate vagueness word, and the vagueness is the point. Arrested in connection with the robbery reports that a person has been linked to it without saying how — which is exactly why police statements and news reports use it, and why an editor should leave it alone there and cut it everywhere else, where about, over, or for does the job in one word. Against in association with, which claims that two things co-occurred, in connection with claims only that something is relevant to a matter.
entries.meaning: Links the statement to a matter without specifying the link. Its usefulness and its emptiness come from the same source: it names a relation and declines to say which one.
examples: Two men were arrested in connection with the break-in.
She was questioned in connection with a series of unpaid invoices.
In connection with the merger, the company disclosed four side agreements.
Costs incurred in connection with the audit are reimbursable.
No charges have been filed in connection with what happened on the tenth.

entries.respell: in KAHN-trast too (noun stress on the first syllable; the verb contrast is /kənˈtræst/)
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in contrast to what the ads suggest). Never a that-clause, and because the to is a preposition, never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: In contrast to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause], in contrast to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Against unlike, which is a single-word preposition doing the same job more economically, and against as opposed to, which adds a note of rejection or correction. Note that the complement must be grammatically parallel to what it is contrasted with, or you get a false comparison: In contrast to the 1990s, today's market is volatile compares a decade to a market.
variants: in contrast with is equally standard. The bare adverbial in contrast (with no complement) is a conjunctive adverb, not a preposition: Sales fell. In contrast, margins improved.
entries.meaning: Sets its object against the main clause as an opposite case. It signals the reader to expect difference, so the two halves must be genuinely comparable.
examples: In contrast to the coasts, the interior stayed dry all summer.
Her second novel, in contrast to the first, is almost cheerful.
In contrast to earlier models, this one runs silently.
The northern district gained population, in contrast to every other part of the state.
In contrast to what the ads suggest, the plan has a deductible.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in exchange for dropping the suit). Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is possible but rare (in exchange for whatever they could salvage).
entries.pattern: [clause] in exchange for [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · In exchange for [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: In exchange of is an error — the noun exchange takes for, not of. Against in return for, which is nearly identical, in exchange for leans toward a transaction with two concrete sides, in return for toward a favor answered. Against plain for, both are explicit about reciprocity. Bare in exchange is an adverbial and takes no object: He gave up the patent and got nothing in exchange.
entries.meaning: Names what is given back in a trade. Both halves of the exchange are stated, which is what distinguishes it from a simple for of price.
examples: He agreed to testify in exchange for immunity.
In exchange for the land, the developer will build a park.
She tutors his kids in exchange for studio space.
The company got tax breaks in exchange for keeping the plant open.
They released the documents in exchange for dropping the lawsuit.

entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (in keeping with what other districts have offered). Never a that-clause; a gerund is possible but awkward.
entries.pattern: [clause], in keeping with [noun phrase]. · In keeping with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Where in accordance with means conformity to a rule that binds, in keeping with means consistency with a spirit, tradition, or character — nobody is obliged. Compare in accordance with the statute (legally required) with in keeping with the family's wishes (fitting, not mandated). In line with sits between the two.
entries.meaning: Says the action fits the tone or precedent of what it follows. It is evaluative rather than regulatory, which is why it collocates with tradition, spirit, character, and wishes.
examples: In keeping with tradition, the outgoing chair gave the closing toast.
The renovation is in keeping with the character of the neighborhood.
In keeping with the family's wishes, the service was private.
His decision was entirely in keeping with everything he had said before.
The pay increase is in keeping with what other districts have offered.

entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (in line with what the committee recommended). Never a that-clause; a gerund is rare.
entries.pattern: [clause] in line with [noun phrase]. · In line with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Weaker than in accordance with (no obligation) and more quantitative than in keeping with — earnings come in in line with expectations. Do not confuse the frozen phrase with the literal in line with the doorframe, meaning physically aligned, which uses the same words and is also current.
entries.meaning: Reports that something matched an expectation, forecast, or policy. It is the standard verb-free way for analysts and reporters to say "as predicted."
examples: Third-quarter results came in in line with analysts' forecasts.
The proposal is broadly in line with what the committee recommended.
In line with company policy, all expenses over $50 require a receipt.
Wage growth is now roughly in line with inflation.
The new rules bring the state in line with federal standards.

entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative (in proportion to what each partner contributed). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] in proportion to [noun phrase]. · In proportion to [noun phrase], [clause]. · directly / inversely in proportion to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: It asserts a ratio, which relative to and compared with do not: wages fell relative to rents says only that one moved against the other, while wages rose in proportion to hours worked says the two move together at a steady rate. Against sense 3 of according to (aid distributed according to need), the two overlap, but in proportion to commits to a measurable ratio where according to commits only to a criterion. The pair to know from science writing is directly in proportion to and inversely in proportion to.
variants: In proportion with is an error — the noun proportion takes to. The negative counterpart is out of proportion to (a fine out of all proportion to the offense), which says the ratio is wrong rather than fixed.
entries.meaning: States that one quantity varies with another at a steady rate. Because it makes a quantitative claim, it should not be reached for loosely where in line with is meant.
examples: Dues are set in proportion to each member's revenue.
Air resistance rises in proportion to the square of the speed.
The penalty should be in proportion to the harm actually done.
Seats are allocated in proportion to population, not land area.
Payouts are calculated in proportion to what each partner contributed.
Their share of the costs falls in proportion to the space they actually use.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in relation to what was agreed in June). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] in relation to [noun phrase]. · In relation to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Sense 1 overlaps with regard to and concerning; sense 2 overlaps relative to and compared with. The two readings can collide — small in relation to the budget is a comparison, questions in relation to the budget is a topic — and only the surrounding words disambiguate. Where sense 1 is meant, about or regarding is almost always tighter.
entries.meaning: 1. Concerning; on the subject of. He was questioned in relation to the break-in. 2. In proportion to; compared with. The fee is small in relation to the total cost.
examples: He was questioned in relation to a burglary in the same block.
The report makes no findings in relation to the second complaint.
In relation to staffing, nothing has been decided.
The fee is trivial in relation to the total cost of the project.
Their salaries have fallen sharply in relation to the cost of living.
The moon's size in relation to Earth is unusual among planets and satellites.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in response to what the auditors found). Never a that-clause, and because this to is a preposition, never a bare infinitive — in response to receiving the notice, not in response to receive.
entries.pattern: In response to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in response to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Causal like because of, but it requires that the object be something addressed to the subject — a question, a request, a crisis that demanded an answer. Because of the rain we canceled is a bare cause; in response to the rain would be odd unless the rain had made a demand. Bare in response is an adverbial with no object: They filed suit. In response, the city rewrote the ordinance.
entries.meaning: Marks the stimulus that the main clause answers. The relation is reactive rather than merely causal, which is why it is standard in official statements and in the methods sections of reports.
examples: In response to the complaints, the airline added two more flights.
Prices rose sharply in response to the supply disruption.
She wrote a four-page memo in response to a two-line email.
In response to your inquiry, the position has been filled.
The agency issued new guidance in response to the court's ruling.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is possible but uncommon (in return for whatever help he could give).
entries.pattern: [clause] in return for [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · In return for [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in exchange for in most sentences; in return for is the better fit when the second party is repaying a favor or a service rather than trading goods. The bare adverbial in return (no complement) is not a preposition: She helped him, and he said nothing in return.
entries.meaning: Names what is given back as compensation or reciprocation. It presupposes that the first party gave something first.
examples: In return for her help, he fixed the transmission.
The union accepted a wage freeze in return for job guarantees.
She asks nothing in return for the work she does at the shelter.
In return for the endorsement, the campaign promised a speaking slot.
They got free housing in return for managing the property.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈdɪnt əv/ · connected speech /baɪ ˈdɪn də/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (by dint of working nights). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] by dint of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · By dint of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Means "by means of, through the force of," and is almost always followed by a noun of effort — hard work, sheer persistence, repetition. Against by virtue of, which cites a qualification or status, by dint of cites exertion. Dint is a fossilized word for "a blow, force" and appears in no other living phrase.
entries.meaning: Attributes an achievement to sustained effort. It is a small, self-consciously literary preposition, and in modern American prose it is close to a set piece.
examples: By dint of sheer persistence, she finally got the records released.
He passed the bar by dint of six months of eighteen-hour days.
The team stayed in contention by dint of an absurd defensive record.
By dint of repetition, the phrase had lost all meaning.
She rose to partner by dint of out-working everyone around her.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈminz əv/ · connected speech /baɪ ˈminz ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] by means of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · By means of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: An explicit by of instrument. Where plain by would be ambiguous between agent and instrument (The lock was opened by the technician versus by a magnet), by means of forces the instrument reading. In ordinary prose, by, with, or using is shorter and just as clear.
entries.meaning: Names the instrument or method that made the action possible. The plural means is invariable here; there is no by mean of.
examples: The sample is heated by means of an induction coil.
Access is controlled by means of a keycard system.
They crossed the ravine by means of a rope bridge.
The message was transmitted by means of a simple substitution cipher.
By means of a series of small loans, the cooperative rebuilt the mill.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈrizən əv/ · connected speech /baɪ ˈrizə nə/
entries.register: legal; largely confined to statutes, pleadings, and verdicts
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically an abstract one naming a condition or a failure (by reason of insanity, by reason of age, by reason of nonpayment). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause. A gerund is possible in drafting (by reason of having failed to appear) but the nominal is preferred.
entries.pattern: [clause] by reason of [noun phrase] · not guilty by reason of [noun phrase] (fixed) · By reason of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A legal because of, and outside legal writing that is what to use. Against by virtue of, which grounds an entitlement in a status the subject holds, by reason of names a cause of liability, exemption, or incapacity — which is why the two split so cleanly in practice: you chair the board by virtue of your office and are excused by reason of illness. The verdict formula not guilty by reason of insanity is fixed and admits no variation; by reason whereof is its archaic drafting relative.
entries.meaning: Attributes a legal consequence to the fact that caused it. Its survival is purely professional: it says nothing because of does not say, and it says it two words longer.
examples: He was found not guilty by reason of insanity.
The lease may be terminated by reason of nonpayment.
No employee may be dismissed by reason of jury service.
By reason of their age, two of the defendants were tried separately.
The claim failed by reason of the plaintiff's own delay.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈvɜrtʃu əv/ · connected speech /baɪ ˈvɜrtʃu ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (by virtue of being a resident). Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is possible but rare (by virtue of what the charter grants him).
entries.pattern: [clause] by virtue of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · By virtue of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Cites a status, office, or inherent property as the reason something holds — by virtue of her office, by virtue of the contract. Against because of, it is narrower: the cause must be something the subject possesses or occupies. Against by dint of, which credits effort, this credits standing. Virtue here means "power, efficacy," not moral goodness.
entries.meaning: Grounds an entitlement or a consequence in a qualifying fact. It is the standard formula for automatic, definitional consequences in legal writing.
examples: By virtue of her office, the mayor chairs the redevelopment board.
Children born here are citizens by virtue of the Fourteenth Amendment.
He inherited the title by virtue of being the eldest son.
The clause is void by virtue of the statute of frauds.
By virtue of its size alone, the company sets the market price.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] by way of [noun phrase / verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Three distinct senses, and they are told apart only by the complement: a place name gives sense 1, an abstract noun of function gives sense 2, an instrument gives sense 3. Against via, sense 1 is the plain-English equivalent. Sense 2 has no one-word substitute — by way of apology means "as an apology," and as alone would not carry the tentativeness.
entries.meaning: 1. Traveling through; via. We flew to Lisbon by way of Newark. 2. As a form of; serving as. He sent flowers by way of apology. 3. By means of. The data reaches the server by way of an encrypted tunnel.
examples: We flew to Lisbon by way of Newark.
The pipeline reaches the coast by way of three pumping stations.
He sent flowers by way of apology.
She offered a shrug by way of explanation.
By way of introduction, let me say how the committee was formed.
The data reaches the server by way of an encrypted tunnel.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ə ˈvju tu/ · weak /wəð ə ˈvju tə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only. The to here is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so with a view to increase costs is wrong — it must be with a view to increasing costs. This is the single most common error with the phrase. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with a view to [verb-ing / noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Means "with the aim of." Against in order to, which takes a bare infinitive (in order to reduce costs), with a view to takes a gerund (with a view to reducing costs). Mixing the two produces the classic error.
variants: with a view toward and with an eye to are American alternatives
with a view to is the standard drafting form. British writers also use with a view towards.
entries.meaning: States the purpose behind an action that is only a first step toward it. It implies the goal is intended but not yet achieved, which is why it is so common in negotiation and planning language.
examples: The parties met with a view to settling the dispute.
The land was purchased with a view to future expansion.
They reorganized the department with a view to cutting overhead.
The bill was drafted with a view to surviving a court challenge.
She took the position with a view to eventually running the program.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (with reference to what you raised on Tuesday). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: With reference to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] with reference to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The letter-opening member of the with ___ to group: sense 1 points back at a specific document or previous communication, where with regard to and with respect to point at a topic generally. Sense 2 is the technical one and is the reason the phrase survives at all — measured with reference to sea level means "using it as the baseline," which with regard to cannot mean. Note also with references to is an error in the topic sense, exactly parallel to with regards to.
entries.meaning: 1. Concerning; further to (a document or previous message). With reference to your letter of April 2, the shipment left on Monday. 2. Measured or defined by taking something as the baseline (technical). All elevations are given with reference to mean sea level.
examples: With reference to your letter of April 2, the shipment left on Monday.
With reference to the matter we discussed, I have spoken to counsel.
With reference to what you raised on Tuesday, the committee has no position yet.
All elevations are given with reference to mean sea level.
The clause must be read with reference to the definitions in Section 1.
Velocity is meaningless except with reference to some frame.
The tolerances are specified with reference to the finished surface, not the blank.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (with regard to what the statute requires). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: with regard to hiring, not with regard to hire.
entries.pattern: With regard to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] with regard to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: With regards to is an error. Regards with an s means greetings (give my regards to your mother), and it belongs at the bottom of a letter, not in the middle of a sentence. The singular regard is the noun meaning "attention, consideration." The same rule kills in regards to and as regards to. Note also that as regards takes no to at all.
variants: in regard to and as regards are equally standard
regarding is the one-word form.
entries.meaning: Introduces the topic the statement is about. It is the formal register's about, and it is nearly always compressible — with regard to the budget is usually just on the budget or about the budget.
examples: With regard to the budget, no decision has been made.
The report says nothing with regard to enforcement.
With regard to your second question, the deadline has not changed.
Policies differ sharply with regard to part-time employees.
She has been careless with regard to deadlines all semester.

entries.register: formal; the standard American form in legal, technical, and academic prose
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (with respect to whether the filing was timely). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: with respect to filing, not with respect to file.
entries.pattern: With respect to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] with respect to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with with regard to as a topic marker, but with respect to also has a technical sense that with regard to lacks: differentiate with respect to x, symmetric with respect to the origin — "taking x as the variable or reference." Note that the phrase has nothing to do with deference; with all due respect is a different expression entirely. And as with with regard to, with respects to is an error — the plural belongs only in pay one's respects.
