variants: Abbreviated w.r.t. in mathematics and engineering. In respect of is the British counterpart
in respect to is a less common American variant.
entries.meaning: 1. On the subject of; as far as X is concerned (topic marker). With respect to the second charge, the jury could not agree. 2. Taking X as the variable, baseline, or axis (technical). Differentiate the function with respect to time.
examples: With respect to the second charge, the jury could not agree.
The statute is silent with respect to electronic filings.
With respect to scheduling, please copy the front office on everything.
The parties remain apart with respect to whether the notice was timely.
Differentiate the function with respect to time.
The two designs are identical with respect to power draw.
The curve is symmetric with respect to the origin.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ði ɪkˈsɛpʃən əv/ · weak /wəð ði ɪkˈsɛpʃən ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a gerund at a pinch (with the exception of having to repaint). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause — the clause-taking form is the conjunction except that.
entries.pattern: With the exception of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] with the exception of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The heaviest member of the exception family. Except for, apart from, aside from, and bare except all do the same work in fewer words. It is worth the length only when the exception needs to be foregrounded, or in drafting where except alone might be read as attaching to the wrong element.
entries.meaning: Subtracts a named item from an otherwise universal claim. The claim must be a genuine generalization; subtracting from a specific statement produces nonsense.
examples: With the exception of Tuesday, the whole week is booked.
Every state, with the exception of Nebraska, has a bicameral legislature.
The building was undamaged, with the exception of two broken windows.
All fees are refundable with the exception of the application charge.
With the exception of one abstention, the vote was unanimous.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ðə ˈhɛlp əv/ · weak /wəð ðə ˈhɛl pə/
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, body, or instrument; a gerund is possible but uncommon. Never a that-clause. A free relative is fine (with the help of whoever happened to be around).
entries.pattern: [clause] with the help of [noun phrase]. · With the help of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Against by means of, which names a pure instrument, with the help of usually names a collaborator and always implies that the subject did the work too — the helper assisted, and did not do it alone. That is also the difference from thanks to, which hands the credit over entirely: We finished thanks to Maria makes her contribution decisive, We finished with the help of Maria makes it partial.
variants: with the aid of is the formal twin and is preferred for instruments (with the aid of a magnifying glass)
with the assistance of is the most formal of the three
with help from is the looser conversational version. The of is not optional, and with the help from is an error.
entries.meaning: Names a contributor to an effort the subject remains responsible for. The main clause keeps the agency; the phrase only shares it.
examples: With the help of two neighbors, they had the roof patched by dark.
She finished the application with the help of a legal aid clinic.
The map was reconstructed with the help of nineteenth-century tax records.
With the help of a state grant, the library stayed open on Sundays.
He got through the first year with the help of whoever would tutor him for free.

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause. Sense 2 also takes a gerund (ahead of leaving), which sense 1 does not.
entries.pattern: [clause] ahead of [noun phrase]. · Ahead of [noun phrase], [clause]. · well/far/just ahead of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against in front of, sense 1 implies a shared line of travel or a queue — the car ahead of us is going the same way, the car in front of us may be parked crosswise. Against before, sense 2 is the journalistic word for anticipation: ahead of the vote rather than before the vote, with an implication of preparation. Bare ahead with no object is an adverb, not this preposition: Go on ahead.
entries.meaning: 1. In front of, in a line or sequence. There were six people ahead of us. 2. Earlier than; in anticipation of. The bill was filed ahead of Friday's deadline. 3. Outperforming; further along than. She finished the year ahead of every projection.
examples: There were six people ahead of us at the counter.
The lead car pulled two lengths ahead of the field.
Markets were jittery ahead of the jobs report.
Ahead of the storm, the county opened four shelters.
Construction is running three weeks ahead of schedule.
She finished the quarter well ahead of every internal projection.
He is years ahead of his classmates in math.

entries.register: neutral; more common in British English than in American, where aside from is preferred
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (apart from being expensive), objective-case pronoun (apart from him), or a nominal wh-clause (apart from what he told me). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: Apart from [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause]. · [clause] apart from [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The same phrase means two opposite things — subtraction (sense 1) and addition (sense 2) — and only context tells them apart: Apart from the noise, it's a good apartment subtracts; Apart from the noise, there's the rent adds. American writers use aside from far more often for both. Note the literal reading too: He stood apart from the group is adverb apart + preposition from, not this unit.
entries.meaning: 1. Except for; leaving aside. Apart from one bad review, the show was a hit. 2. In addition to; besides. Apart from the salary, there's a housing allowance.
examples: Apart from one bad review, the show was a hit.
I know nothing about her apart from her name.
Apart from being expensive, the software is genuinely hard to use.
Apart from the salary, there's a housing allowance and a car.
Who came, apart from the two of you?
Apart from that, how was the trip?

entries.register: neutral; the standard American form where British English says apart from
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, objective-case pronoun, or a nominal wh-clause (aside from what you already know). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: Aside from [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause]. · [clause] aside from [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning and in double sense to apart from — it both subtracts and adds — and differs only in national preference. Against except for, which only subtracts, aside from is ambiguous, so use except for when the exception reading has to be unmistakable. Bare aside is an adverb and takes no object — Step aside, She set the money aside, joking aside — where aside from always requires one; the two words cannot be separated.
entries.meaning: 1. Except for. Aside from a sore knee, he came through the season fine. 2. In addition to. Aside from the fine, you lose four points on your license.
examples: Aside from a sore knee, he came through the season fine.
Aside from Tuesday, I'm free all week.
There's nothing in the fridge aside from condiments.
Aside from the fine, you lose four points on your license.
Aside from being the cheapest option, it's also the fastest.
Aside from that, I have no complaints.

entries.ipa: /æt ði ɪkˈspɛns əv/ · weak /ət ði ɪkˈspɛn sə/ — at reduces to /ət/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (at the expense of losing accuracy). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] at the expense of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · [what was gained], at the expense of [what was given up]
entries.contrast: The two senses are told apart by the object: money and a payer give sense 1, a value or an injured party gives sense 2. Sense 2 is the commoner one in writing and always asserts a completed trade-off — speed at the expense of accuracy claims accuracy was actually lost, which is a stronger claim than rather than or instead of would make. Do not confuse it with the fixed phrase a joke at his expense, where the person is the target rather than the payer.
entries.meaning: 1. Paid for by. The trip was made at the expense of the foundation. 2. With a loss or sacrifice of; to the detriment of. The plant gained speed at the expense of accuracy.
examples: The trip was made at the expense of the foundation, not the taxpayers.
Repairs were carried out at the expense of the previous owner.
The redesign gained speed at the expense of readability.
Growth came at the expense of every small grower in the valley.
He built the department at the expense of his own research.
They shortened the timeline at the expense of testing anything properly.

entries.ipa: /æt ðə ˈhændz əv/ · weak /ət ðə ˈhændz ə/ — at reduces to /ət/
entries.register: formal to neutral; news writing, history, and sports reporting
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a person, group, or institution — never an inanimate force. Never a that-clause, never a gerund. A free relative naming an agent is fine (at the hands of whoever was guarding him).
entries.pattern: [noun of harm or defeat] at the hands of [person or body] · [clause] at the hands of [person or body]
entries.contrast: An agentive phrase with a restriction built into it: what happens at somebody's hands is always something bad. A beating at the hands of the guards and a defeat at the hands of an unranked team are idiomatic; a gift at the hands of her uncle is not, and plain by is the neutral form for everything else. It also insists on a human or corporate agent, which is why damage at the hands of the storm is a misuse where damage from the storm is right — compare at the mercy of, which takes forces freely because it reports powerlessness rather than injury. Note that hands is invariable: there is no at the hand of in this sense.
entries.meaning: Names the agent responsible for harm, defeat, or mistreatment. The main clause supplies the injury and the phrase supplies who inflicted it, which is why it cannot be used where nothing bad occurred.
examples: The team suffered its worst loss of the season at the hands of an unranked opponent.
Hundreds died at the hands of the regime in the first month alone.
She described years of mistreatment at the hands of a former employer.
The manuscript met a sorry end at the hands of an overzealous editor.
The measure died at the hands of the very committee that drafted it.
He lost the title at the hands of a fighter nobody had heard of in March.

entries.ipa: /æt ðə ˈmɜrsi əv/ · weak /ət ðə ˈmɜrsi ə/ — at reduces to /ət/
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, body, or uncontrollable force. Never a that-clause, never a gerund. A free relative is fine and is common (at the mercy of whatever the wholesalers decide to pay).
entries.pattern: be at the mercy of [noun phrase] · leave someone at the mercy of [noun phrase] · entirely/completely/utterly at the mercy of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: It asserts powerlessness, not cruelty — at the mercy of the weather accuses the weather of nothing, and the phrase is fully idiomatic with forces that have no intentions at all. That is what separates it from at the hands of, which requires an agent and requires that harm actually occurred: you are at the mercy of a landlord before anything happens and at the hands of one only after it does. The related expressions have mercy on and without mercy are ordinary noun uses and not this preposition.
entries.meaning: Places the subject under something it cannot control. What follows may be a person with power or a force with none — the phrase cares only that the subject cannot resist it.
examples: Small growers are at the mercy of whatever the wholesalers decide to pay.
The lifeboat was at the mercy of the current for nine hours.
Without the subsidy, the clinic is at the mercy of private donors.
The schedule leaves the whole project at the mercy of a single supplier.
Renters here are completely at the mercy of a market with no vacancies.
He refused to be at the mercy of a committee that met twice a year.

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative is fine (away from what she had grown up with). Sense 3 takes a measure phrase before it (two blocks away from).
entries.pattern: [clause] away from [noun phrase] · [measure] away from [noun phrase] · Away from [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Away alone is an adverb (She's away this week); the preposition needs from and an object. Against bare from, away from stresses separation and increasing distance rather than origin: He came from Detroit names a source, He moved away from Detroit describes a departure.
entries.meaning: 1. Moving so as to increase distance. She backed slowly away from the dog. 2. Separated from; not in the company of. He is different away from his family. 3. At a stated distance or remove (with a measure phrase). The school is two blocks away from here.
examples: She backed slowly away from the dog.
Keep the heater away from the curtains.
He is a completely different person away from the office.
Away from the tourist streets, the city is quiet.
The nearest hospital is forty minutes away from the site.
We're one win away from the playoffs.
She has spent ten years moving away from what she was raised to believe.

entries.register: neutral — the default causal preposition of American English
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (because of being late), or a nominal wh-clause (because of who he knows, because of what the inspector found). Never a that-clause — because alone is the conjunction that takes a clause (because it rained), and because of it rained is impossible.
entries.pattern: [clause] because of [noun phrase]. · Because of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Because + clause versus because of + noun phrase is the cleanest preposition/conjunction pair in English: We stayed home because it rained / We stayed home because of the rain. Against due to, because of is adverbial and never disputed; against owing to and on account of, it is the plain, unmarked choice. The internet-era because noun (because science) is a deliberate joke and is not standard.
entries.meaning: Names the cause of the event in the main clause. It modifies the verb or the whole clause, which is exactly what distinguishes it from due to in the traditional rule.
examples: The flight was canceled because of fog.
Because of the strike, deliveries are running two days late.
She missed the deadline because of a family emergency.
He got the job because of who he knows, not what he knows.
Because of being out of the country, he never received the notice.
Attendance dropped because of the parking situation.

entries.register: neutral in sense 1; informal and usually ironic in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, almost always naming a person, body, or organization; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative naming an agent is idiomatic in sense 2 (courtesy of whoever left the gate open).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], courtesy of [noun phrase]. · [clause] courtesy of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is an attribution formula that presumes permission was granted — photograph courtesy of the state archive. Sense 2 has drifted into sarcasm and thanks nobody: a two-hour delay, courtesy of the airline. Against thanks to, which is also ironizable, courtesy of keeps a note of formal crediting even when the tone is bitter.
variants: by courtesy of is the older full form and survives in formal credit lines
American English has generally dropped the by.
entries.meaning: 1. Given, lent, or supplied by (a credit line). All images courtesy of the Newberry Library. 2. As the result of (often unwelcome). We got a flooded basement, courtesy of the city's storm drains.
examples: All photographs are courtesy of the state historical society.
The venue was donated courtesy of a local foundation.
Dinner is courtesy of the hotel, since they lost our reservation.
We got a flooded basement, courtesy of the city's storm drains.
Another three-hour delay, courtesy of the airline's scheduling.
He has a permanent limp, courtesy of one bad tackle in 1998.
The whole hallway smells like smoke, courtesy of whoever propped the fire door open.

entries.complement: noun phrase only, and characteristically an abstract mass noun (devoid of humor, devoid of merit). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund. It cannot stand without of — there is no the room was devoid.
entries.pattern: be devoid of [noun phrase] · [noun] devoid of [noun phrase] · entirely/utterly/wholly devoid of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Stronger and more literary than without or lacking: devoid of asserts total absence, not mere shortage. Against void of, which is archaic outside legal boilerplate, devoid of is the living form. Against free of, which is positive (free of charge), devoid of is negative or critical.
entries.meaning: Declares a complete absence of some quality. Because it is absolute, it resists hedging — somewhat devoid of is a solecism — but it takes intensifiers freely.
examples: The argument is utterly devoid of evidence.
His prose is elegant but entirely devoid of warmth.
The room was devoid of furniture except for a folding chair.
The claim is devoid of any legal merit.
She delivered the line devoid of inflection.

entries.register: neutral — different from is the American standard
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (different from me, never different from I), gerund (different from working nights), or a free relative (different from what I expected). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [X] is different from [Y] · very / completely / no different from [noun phrase] · [noun] different from [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The whole rule in one line: from before a noun, from what or than before a clause, never to in American writing. The reason from is the default is the verb behind the adjective — one thing differs from another, and nobody writes differs than. Against similar to, its exact opposite, the pair is worth memorizing together, because English hands the two comparison adjectives opposite prepositions and gives no reason for it. Against unlike, which is a one-word preposition doing the same job, different from is predicative where unlike is not: Unlike her sister, she plays cannot be rewritten as Different from her sister, she plays.
variants: Different than is standard American English before a clause, where it saves a heavy from what: The result was different than I expected is accepted everywhere, and different from what I expected is the longer, unimpeachable form. Before a plain noun phrase — different than me, different than the others — it is the form editors change, and from is what to write. Different to is British and Australian and does not belong in American prose.
entries.meaning: States non-identity between two things. It is freely gradable — slightly different from, no different from, completely different from — which is what keeps different a live adjective rather than a frozen particle.
examples: Her second album is completely different from the first.
Teaching adults is different from teaching eight-year-olds.
The rules are different from the ones we trained on.
The result was different from what anyone had predicted.
His account is not materially different from hers.
This model is no different from last year's except for the badge.
Nothing about the second inspection was different from the first.

entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [statement of amount] exclusive of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The direct opposite of inclusive of, and the pair is the standard way to fix the boundaries of a quoted figure: $400 exclusive of tax versus $400 inclusive of tax. Against except for and apart from, this one is confined to quantities and lists — you cannot say exclusive of that, I enjoyed it.
entries.meaning: Excludes an item from a stated total. It is a pricing and drafting word, and outside those contexts not including is better.
examples: The rate is $180 a night exclusive of tax and resort fees.
The team has eleven employees exclusive of contractors.
Damages are capped at $50,000 exclusive of interest and costs.
Delivery takes four business days exclusive of weekends.
The budget totals $2.1 million exclusive of capital expenditures.

entries.complement: noun phrase in sense 1; an adjective, a noun, or a gerund in sense 2 (far from perfect, far from a solution, far from being finished); a free relative in either (far from what we were promised). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] far from [noun phrase] · be far from [adjective / noun / verb-ing] · Far from [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause].
entries.contrast: Sense 2 is a negator, not a distance word. Far from perfect means "not perfect at all," and the fronted form — Far from helping, the new rule made things worse — denies the first idea and asserts its opposite, so a learner who reads it as a comparison gets the sentence exactly backwards. Against away from, which describes motion or growing separation, far from states a distance already in place: you move away from the coast and then live far from it. Bare far is an adverb and takes no object (We didn't go far, far too expensive), and the fixed reply far from it, meaning "not at all," takes the invariable pronoun and nothing else.
entries.meaning: 1. At a great distance from (literal). They live far from the nearest hospital. 2. Not at all; the opposite of (with an adjective, noun, or gerund). The building is far from finished.
examples: They live far from the nearest hospital.
Far from the tourist streets, the prices drop by half.
The building is far from finished.
The evidence is far from conclusive.
Far from helping, the new rule made the backlog worse.
Her explanation was far from what the committee had been told.
"Was it easy?" "Far from it."

entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund. Sense 2 requires a duration noun (inside of an hour).
entries.pattern: [clause] inside of [noun phrase] · inside of [duration]
entries.contrast: In the spatial sense the of is optional and usually edited out — inside the house is preferred to inside of the house in edited American prose, and British usage rejects the of outright. In the time sense, however, inside of an hour is an established American idiom that inside an hour only partly replaces, and within an hour is the neutral alternative. Bare inside with no object is an adverb: Let's go inside.
entries.meaning: 1. Within the interior of (spatial; the of is dispensable). He kept the receipts inside of a shoebox. 2. In less than (a stated span of time; American idiom). They had the road cleared inside of two hours.
examples: He kept every receipt inside of a shoebox.
There was nothing inside of the envelope but a photograph.
Something inside of me knew it was a bad idea.
They had the road cleared inside of two hours.
The whole thing was over inside of a week.
You won't find a better price inside of fifty miles.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (instead of driving), or a nominal wh-clause (instead of what you ordered). Never a bare infinitive — instead of to drive is wrong — and never a that-clause. Note that it does take a full prepositional phrase in the parallel-contrast pattern: We met at the office instead of at the diner.
entries.pattern: [clause] instead of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · Instead of [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause].
entries.contrast: Instead of is the preposition and needs an object; bare instead is an adverb and takes none — We took the bus instead is correct, We took the bus instead of is not. Against in place of and in lieu of, it is the plain, unrestricted choice and the only one that takes a gerund comfortably in speech. Against rather than, which can join two verbs directly (rather than complain), instead of must nominalize (instead of complaining).
entries.meaning: Replaces one option with another. Both options must be grammatically parallel — the commonest error is a mismatch, as in Instead of the bus, he walked, where a noun is being contrasted with a verb.
examples: Let's take the train instead of driving.
She ordered soup instead of the salad.
Instead of complaining, try filing a report.
He spent the afternoon reading instead of studying.
We met at the office instead of at the diner.
Instead of one long meeting, we'll have three short ones.

entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (irrespective of what the survey shows). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] irrespective of [noun phrase / wh-clause]. · Irrespective of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Synonymous with regardless of, which is far more common in American English; irrespective of is the formal, legal-flavored twin. Note that irrespective is the correct word with the ir- prefix — the nonstandard irregardless is a blend of these two and should never be written.
entries.meaning: Dismisses a factor as irrelevant to what the main clause asserts. It is the drafting word for non-discrimination clauses and eligibility rules.
examples: The benefit is available to all employees irrespective of length of service.
Irrespective of cost, the repair has to be done this month.
Admission is open to applicants irrespective of nationality.
The rule applies irrespective of what the parties intended.
Irrespective of the outcome, the process was worth it.

entries.ipa: /ɑn əˈkaʊnt əv/ · connected speech /ɑn əˈkaʊn də/
entries.register: neutral to formal in standard use; the clause-taking version is regional and nonstandard
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (on account of being sick), or a nominal wh-clause (on account of what he said). A that-clause or a bare finite clause after it — on account of he was sick — is nonstandard in writing, though it is well attested in Southern and Appalachian speech and in dialogue.
entries.pattern: [clause] on account of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · On account of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A three-word because of, slightly more formal in writing and slightly folksier in speech, depending on the surrounding register. Against due to, it is safely adverbial. Note the unrelated literal phrase on account meaning "as partial payment" ($50 on account), which is accounting language, not this preposition.
entries.meaning: Gives the reason for the main clause. In edited American prose because of is the default and on account of is a stylistic choice; in speech it often signals a homelier register.
examples: The game was called on account of rain.
She retired early on account of her back.
On account of the holiday, the office closes at noon.
He was excused on account of being the only caregiver at home.
The road is closed on account of flooding.

entries.ipa: /ɑn bɪˈhæf əv/ · connected speech /ɑn bɪˈhæ və/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, naming a person or body; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative naming a person is fine (on behalf of whoever ends up holding the lease).
entries.pattern: [clause] on behalf of [noun phrase]. · On behalf of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Against for, this specifies representation rather than mere benefit. Against in the name of, which invokes authority, on behalf of names a principal you are acting for. The reflexive form is on my own behalf, not on behalf of myself.
variants: in behalf of was traditionally distinguished in American usage — on behalf of = "as the agent of," in behalf of = "for the benefit of" — but the distinction has largely collapsed and on behalf of now covers both. In behalf of is safe to avoid.
entries.meaning: Marks the person or body the speaker or actor is representing. It is the standard opening of formal remarks and the standard signature line of counsel and agents.
examples: On behalf of the entire staff, thank you for twenty years.
The attorney filed the motion on behalf of her client.
He accepted the award on behalf of his late father.
The union bargains on behalf of eleven thousand members.
On behalf of the mayor, I'd like to welcome you to the city.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈbeɪsɪs əv/ · connected speech /ɑn ðə ˈbeɪsɪ sə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (on the basis of what he saw). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the basis of [noun phrase]. · On the basis of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Names the evidence or criterion a judgment rests on, where because of names a cause. Hired on the basis of her portfolio describes the grounds for a decision; hired because of her portfolio describes what made it happen. Non-discrimination law makes heavy use of on the basis of precisely because "grounds" is the legally relevant idea.
variants: on the basis that is the clause-taking companion form and is a conjunction, not this preposition: on the basis that the contract had lapsed.
entries.meaning: Identifies what a decision, claim, or classification was grounded in. It is the standard formula in statutes, methods sections, and administrative findings.
examples: Applicants are ranked on the basis of test scores and interviews.
Discrimination on the basis of age is prohibited.
On the basis of the sample, the estimate is within two points.
The claim was denied on the basis of a paperwork error.
She was hired on the basis of what her references said, not her résumé.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈɡraʊndz əv/ · connected speech /ɑn ðə ˈɡraʊnd zə/
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a recognized ground — age, race, national origin, cost, ill health, national security — or a free relative (on the grounds of what the inspector found). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the grounds of [noun phrase] · refuse / object / dismiss / discriminate on the grounds of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Exactly parallel to on the basis of, and the two are near-interchangeable in discrimination law, but on the grounds of leans toward a reason given for refusing, objecting, or excluding, while on the basis of leans toward a criterion used for deciding: you are hired on the basis of your record and dismissed on the grounds of misconduct. Against because of, this one claims the reason was formally stated, not merely operative.
variants: on grounds of, without the article, is common in headlines and drafting

the singular on the ground of is older and now rare in American use. The clause-taking companion is on the grounds that + a full clause (on the grounds that the notice was late), which is a conjunction and not this preposition — the same split as in case of / in case and on the basis of / on the basis that.
entries.meaning: Names the stated reason for a decision, an objection, or a refusal. The reason is presented as one the speaker is prepared to defend, which is why the phrase belongs to rulings and appeals rather than to ordinary explanation.
examples: The application was refused on the grounds of cost.
Discrimination on the grounds of age is unlawful in every state.
He objected on the grounds of relevance.
She retired early on the grounds of ill health.
The documents were withheld on the grounds of national security.
The appeal succeeded on the grounds of what the trial transcript actually showed.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈhilz əv/ · connected speech /ɑn ðə ˈhil zə/
entries.register: neutral to formal; a standard idiom of news writing
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an event; a gerund is possible but uncommon (on the heels of losing the contract). Never a that-clause. A free relative naming the event is fine (on the heels of what happened in March).
entries.pattern: come/follow/arrive on the heels of [noun phrase] · [clause], on the heels of [noun phrase] · hard/hot on the heels of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against in the wake of, the phrase it is most often confused with, this one claims closeness in time and nothing more: in the wake of the scandal says the scandal caused what followed, while on the heels of the scandal says only that the second thing came fast behind the first. Reach for in the wake of when you mean consequence and on the heels of when you mean the very next thing. Against plain after, both add speed and neither is neutral.
variants: hard on the heels of and hot on the heels of are the intensified forms and mean "immediately after." Heels is invariable — there is no on the heel of.
entries.meaning: Marks an event as following hard upon another. The metaphor is pursuit, so the two events have to be close enough together for the second to be treading on the first.
examples: The layoffs came on the heels of a record quarter.
On the heels of the recall, two more suppliers suspended shipments.
The announcement arrived hard on the heels of the mayor's resignation.
A second storm followed on the heels of the first.
On the heels of losing the contract, the firm closed its Denver office.
The bill passed on the heels of three years of failed attempts.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈpɑrt əv/ · connected speech /ɑn ðə ˈpɑr də/
entries.register: formal; legal, academic, and report writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a person or a body — never a thing. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun of conduct or attitude] on the part of [person or body] · There was no [noun] on the part of [person].
entries.contrast: Its one job is to attach an actor to an abstract noun of behavior — negligence, reluctance, failure, bad faith, misunderstanding — where the nominalization has lost the subject a verb would have carried: negligence on the part of the contractor is the contractor was negligent, kept nominal. That is also its weakness, since nine times in ten a by phrase or a plain verb is shorter. The complement must be animate — a failure on the part of the software is a misuse for a failure of the software. Do not confuse it with for my part ("as far as I'm concerned") or take the part of ("side with"), which are separate fixed phrases.
entries.meaning: Assigns an abstract behavior to the person or body responsible for it. It exists because English nominalizations drop their subjects, and this is the phrase that puts one back.
examples: There was no bad faith on the part of either side.
The report found negligence on the part of two supervisors.
Some reluctance on the part of the family is understandable.
It was a genuine misunderstanding on the part of the clerk.
Any failure on the part of the tenant to give notice voids the clause.
The delay reflects real indecision on the part of the board.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈstrɛŋkθ əv/ · also /ˈstrɛŋθ/ · connected speech /ɑn ðə ˈstrɛŋk θə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative (on the strength of what the scouts reported). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the strength of [noun phrase]. · On the strength of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Against on the basis of, which names a criterion neutrally, on the strength of adds that the thing named was persuasive enough to carry the decision: hired on the basis of her portfolio says the portfolio was what they looked at, hired on the strength of her portfolio says it was what convinced them. Against because of, it confines the cause to evidence, testimony, or a record that somebody actually weighed. It resists a weak object — on the strength of a rumor reads as deliberate irony, and that irony is the proof of the rule.
entries.meaning: Names the evidence or achievement that carried a decision. It presupposes that somebody was persuaded, which is why it attaches to hirings, loans, verdicts, promotions, and signings.
examples: The loan was approved on the strength of two years of receipts.
She was promoted on the strength of a single quarter.
On the strength of his testimony, the charges were refiled.
The band was signed on the strength of a four-song demo.
The town rebuilt its budget on the strength of what the new plant paid in taxes.
He got the fellowship on the strength of one unpublished chapter.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈvɜrdʒ əv/ · connected speech /ɑn ðə ˈvɜr dʒə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (on the verge of collapse, on the verge of collapsing). Because of is a preposition, on the verge of to collapse is wrong, and so is on the verge to collapse. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: be on the verge of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · bring/push someone to the verge of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against sense 3 of close to (close to tears), which is gradable and vague about the outcome, on the verge of names a threshold about to be crossed, and it takes only outcomes, never places: close to the airport is fine, on the verge of the airport is nonsense. Against in danger of, it is neutral about whether the outcome is welcome — you can be on the verge of a breakthrough as easily as a breakdown, where in danger of is always bad.
variants: on the brink of is the near-twin and is preferred for large disasters (on the brink of war)

on the point of is the more formal, British-leaning version and takes the same gerund. The of is not optional — the elliptical She was on the verge survives only where the complement has just been said.
entries.meaning: Places the subject one step short of a change of state. Because the change has not happened, the phrase stays true even if it never does.
examples: The company was on the verge of bankruptcy when the order came in.
She was on the verge of tears and would not look up.
Researchers say they are on the verge of a usable test.
He was on the verge of quitting when the transfer came through.
Two of the three species are on the verge of disappearing from the river.
The talks are on the verge of collapse for the third time this year.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund in sense 2 (on top of paying rent). Sense 3 also takes a nominal wh-clause (on top of what the auditors want). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] on top of [noun phrase] · On top of [noun phrase], [clause]. · right on top of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is literal and takes intensifiers (right on top of); senses 2 and 3 are frozen idioms. Against in addition to, sense 2 is the informal equivalent and usually carries a complaint — things pile on top of each other. Against above, sense 1 requires contact: a lamp above the table is not touching it; a book on top of the table is. Bare on top is an adverb, not this preposition, and takes no object: The cake had berries on top is complete; on top of the cake needs its object.
entries.meaning: 1. Resting on the upper surface of. The keys are on top of the refrigerator. 2. In addition to (usually burdensome). On top of everything else, the car wouldn't start. 3. In full control of; up to date with. She stays on top of every deadline.
examples: The keys are on top of the refrigerator.
The truck stopped right on top of the crosswalk.
Stack the folders on top of the printer for now.
On top of everything else, the furnace quit.
On top of paying rent, they cover their own utilities.
She stays on top of every deadline without visible effort.
The manager is completely on top of the situation.

entries.register: neutral — one of the most frequent prepositions in the language
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund in sense 5 only (out of not wanting to offend anyone). In senses 4 and 5 the complement is characteristically a bare mass or abstract noun (out of milk, out of curiosity). Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is possible in sense 2 (out of what little was left).
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] out of [noun phrase] · be out of [noun phrase] · [number] out of [number] · made out of [material]
entries.contrast: Out alone is an adverb or a verb particle and takes no object (She went out, Cross it out); out of is the preposition and requires one. Against from, sense 1 insists on prior enclosure — you come out of a building but from a city. Against of, sense 3 (made out of wood) stresses transformation of raw material, where made of wood just names the substance.
entries.meaning: 1. Moving from inside to outside. She walked out of the room without a word. 2. From (a source, origin, or material). The whole sculpture is carved out of a single log. 3. From a set of (with numbers). Three out of four dentists said the same thing. 4. No longer having; lacking. We're out of coffee. 5. From (a motive). He apologized out of habit rather than conviction. 6. Beyond the limits of (a range or state). The plane was already out of sight. 7. Absent from (a place the subject belongs to or is expected at). She's out of the office until Monday.
examples: She walked out of the room without a word.
Get the dog out of the kitchen.
The whole sculpture is carved out of a single log.
He built the shed out of salvaged lumber.
Three out of four respondents said they would pay more.
She scored 92 out of 100.
We're out of coffee and nearly out of milk.
The team is out of contention for the first time in years.
He apologized out of habit rather than conviction.
I only asked out of curiosity.
The plane was already out of sight.
Your call is out of the ordinary, and so is the answer.
She made supper out of what little was left in the pantry.
He said nothing, out of not wanting to make it worse.
She's out of the office until Monday and unreachable before that.
He has been out of the country since June.

entries.register: neutral in sense 1 (with the of often edited out); informal and chiefly American in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (sense 2: outside of going to the store), or a nominal wh-clause (outside of what has already been said). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] outside of [noun phrase] · Outside of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: In the spatial sense the of is optional and edited American prose usually drops it — outside the building, not outside of the building. Sense 2, meaning "except for," is an Americanism that many editors also cut in favor of aside from or except for, but it is fully idiomatic in speech. Bare outside is an adverb: Wait outside.
entries.meaning: 1. Beyond the limits of (spatial or figurative; the of is dispensable). The plant is outside of the city limits. 2. Except for; apart from (American, informal). Outside of a sore shoulder, I feel fine.
examples: The plant is just outside of the city limits.
That question falls outside of the committee's mandate.
She has no life outside of work.
Outside of a sore shoulder, I feel fine.
Outside of Chicago, he's never lived in a big city.
There's nothing to do here outside of fish and read.

entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (regardless of what happens, regardless of whether he agrees). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] regardless of [noun phrase / wh-clause]. · Regardless of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Irregardless is not a word in standard English — it is a blend of irrespective and regardless, and although dictionaries record it, it is stigmatized everywhere and should never be written. Against in spite of and despite, regardless of dismisses a factor as irrelevant rather than conceding it as an obstacle: in spite of the cost admits the cost was a problem, regardless of the cost refuses to weigh it. Bare regardless is an adverb: He went anyway, regardless.
entries.meaning: Declares a factor immaterial to what the main clause asserts. Because it takes wh-clauses freely, it is unusually flexible for a complex preposition.
examples: The policy applies to all students regardless of age.
Regardless of the weather, the parade steps off at noon.
She'll say the same thing regardless of who is in the room.
The fee is due regardless of whether you attend.
Regardless of cost, this has to be fixed before winter.
He was going to resign regardless of the vote.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (short of firing him), or a nominal wh-clause (short of what organizers predicted). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: be short of [noun phrase] · [clause] short of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · just/well/little short of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Three senses that share a metaphor of falling before a line. Sense 3, "apart from doing," is the one learners miss: Short of selling the house, we've tried everything means "we have tried everything except that." Against out of, sense 1 means "not enough," where out of means "none at all" — short of milk versus out of milk. Bare short is an adjective or adverb and takes no object: We came up short, He stopped short, The fund is short again — where short of always requires one.
entries.meaning: 1. Not having enough of. We're two people short of a quorum. 2. Falling below or before (a mark). The kick landed just short of the goal line. 3. Except for; apart from (an extreme measure). Short of a miracle, the bill is dead.
examples: We're two people short of a quorum.
The nonprofit is badly short of volunteers this year.
The kick landed just short of the goal line.
Turnout was well short of what organizers predicted.
Short of a miracle, the bill is dead this session.
Short of selling the house, we've tried everything.
The performance was little short of astonishing.

entries.register: archaic and literary; survives in legal boilerplate
entries.complement: noun phrase only, almost always abstract. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be void of [noun phrase] · [noun] void of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Devoid of is the living modern form and should be preferred in every ordinary context; void of now reads as poetic or as legal survival. Do not confuse with the legal adjective void meaning "of no effect" (the contract is void), which takes no of.
entries.meaning: Declares emptiness of a quality. Where devoid of still functions in edited prose, void of signals deliberate archaism.
examples: His face was void of expression.
The landscape was void of color for four straight months.
The reply was polite and entirely void of content.
He looked at her with eyes void of recognition.
The document is void of any signature or seal.

entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (according to what she told me). Never a that-clause and never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: According to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause], according to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: According to me is not idiomatic — the phrase attributes a claim to an outside source, so a speaker attributing a claim to himself must say in my opinion or I think. Against in accordance with, which reports conformity to a rule, according to reports what a source says. Sense 3 (according to need) is a distinct, older sense meaning "in proportion to."
entries.meaning: 1. As stated or reported by (a source). According to the coroner, death was instantaneous. 2. In conformity with (a plan, rule, or standard). Everything went according to plan. 3. In proportion to. Aid is distributed according to need.
examples: According to the National Weather Service, the storm turns north tonight.
He's leaving in June, according to two people familiar with the decision.
According to what she told me, the deal fell through in March.
Everything went according to plan until the second act.
Sort the files according to date, not alphabetically.
Aid is distributed according to need rather than population.
Members are taxed according to their ability to pay.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only. The to is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so accustomed to work nights is wrong — it must be accustomed to working nights. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause. The reflexive verb form accustom oneself to follows exactly the same rule: accustom yourself to waiting, never to wait.
entries.pattern: be/grow/become accustomed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · [noun] accustomed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · quite/hardly/not yet accustomed to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This is the cleanest test case in the file for the prepositional to. Substitute a plain noun: accustomed to the noise is perfectly good, which proves the to is a preposition and forces the -ing on any verb that follows. The same test convicts look forward to hearing and object to being questioned. Against given to (given to exaggeration), which reports a tendency, accustomed to reports habituation through repeated exposure. Against familiar with, which is about knowledge, this is about tolerance.
variants: used to is the everyday equivalent and takes the identical complement — used to living alone, never used to live alone in this sense. Beware the trap: used to + bare infinitive (He used to live alone) is a completely different item, a past-habitual auxiliary, and the collision of the two is the reason learners produce I'm used to live here.
entries.meaning: Says the subject has been worn into acceptance of something by exposure to it. It is freely gradable — more accustomed, not yet accustomed, thoroughly accustomed — which is what still marks accustomed as a live adjective rather than a fully frozen particle.
examples: She is accustomed to working nights and sleeps through the afternoon.
He never grew accustomed to the cold.
Readers accustomed to the old layout complained for months.
They are not accustomed to being questioned.
It took a full year to become accustomed to the altitude.
A jury accustomed to long trials would not have found this one unusual.
He is quite accustomed to having his calls returned within the hour.

entries.respell: KLOHSS too — the s is /s/, not /z/; /kloʊz/ is the verb close
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund in sense 3 (close to quitting), or a nominal wh-clause (close to what we expected). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: close to finishing, not close to finish.
entries.pattern: be close to [noun phrase] · [clause] close to [noun phrase] · very/quite/awfully close to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against near, which is a one-word preposition doing the same spatial job, close to is more freely gradable (much closer to, closest to). Against next to, which requires adjacency with nothing in between, close to only requires proximity. Sense 2 with a number means "approximately" and is not spatial at all, and sense 4 is not spatial either — close to her sister is about intimacy, not distance, and it is the one sense that cannot take a measure phrase. Bare close is an adjective or adverb and takes no object — Stay close, That was close — and it is pronounced the same /kloʊs/; only close to is the preposition.
entries.meaning: 1. Near in space. They live close to the airport. 2. Nearly (with a quantity). Close to four hundred people showed up. 3. On the verge of. She was close to tears. 4. Emotionally attached to. She has always been close to her grandmother.
examples: They live close to the airport, which is why the rent is low.
Pull the chair close to the table.
The two candidates finished remarkably close to each other.
Close to four hundred people showed up for a room that seats two hundred.
The repair will run close to three thousand dollars.
She was close to tears by the end of the hearing.
He came close to quitting twice that year.
She has always been close to her grandmother.
He is not especially close to anyone in the family.

entries.respell: KAHN-trair-ee too (stress on the first syllable; the adjective meaning "perverse" is /kənˈtrɛri/, kun-TRAIR-ee)
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause — and the wh-clause is one of its commonest patterns (contrary to what you may have heard, contrary to what the label says). Never a that-clause, never a gerund, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: Contrary to [noun phrase / wh-clause], [clause]. · [clause], contrary to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Sense 2 is the fixed rhetorical opener contrary to popular belief, which corrects the reader; sense 1 is a plainer statement of conflict with a rule or expectation. Against in contrast to, which merely sets two things side by side, contrary to asserts that one contradicts the other. Note the stress difference between this word and the adjective contrary meaning "stubborn." The bare adverbials are separate items: on the contrary rejects what was just said (On the contrary, sales rose), and to the contrary modifies a noun (evidence to the contrary); neither takes an object the way contrary to does.
entries.meaning: 1. In conflict with (a rule, instruction, or fact). The parts were installed contrary to the manufacturer's instructions. 2. Unlike what is generally supposed. Contrary to popular belief, the building is not the tallest in the city.
examples: The parts were installed contrary to the manufacturer's instructions.
He acted contrary to the advice of every lawyer in the room.
Nothing in the record is contrary to her account.
Contrary to popular belief, most avalanches are triggered by the victims.
Contrary to expectations, the smaller school won by nineteen.
The evidence runs contrary to the prosecution's theory.
Contrary to what you may have heard, the branch is not closing.
Contrary to what the label says, the product contains no juice at all.

entries.register: neutral, with a live usage dispute over sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (due to being understaffed), or a nominal wh-clause (due to what the inspector found). Never a that-clause — write due to the fact that if you need one, though because is better. Because this to is a preposition, never a bare infinitive in the causal sense: due to needing repairs, not due to need repairs.
entries.pattern: be due to [noun phrase] · [noun] due to [noun phrase] · Due to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: The classic test: due to is traditionally adjectival, so it should be substitutable by attributable to or caused by and should attach to a noun — The delay was due to fog (fine, due to modifies delay). Using it adverbially to modify a whole clause — Due to fog, the flight was canceled — was condemned for most of the twentieth century, and because of or owing to was prescribed instead. That adverbial use is now standard in American English and appears in edited prose everywhere, but conservative editors still flag it, so because of is the safe choice in formal writing. Note separately that be due to + bare infinitive (The train is due to arrive at six) is a different construction entirely — adjective due plus a true infinitive, meaning "scheduled."
entries.meaning: 1. Caused by; attributable to (adjectival, after be or modifying a noun). The delay was due to fog. 2. Because of (adverbial, modifying the clause — standard but contested). Due to fog, the flight was canceled.
examples: The delay was due to fog over the bay.
Most of the increase is due to a change in how the data is collected.
Absences due to illness must be reported by 9 a.m.
Due to the holiday, there will be no pickup on Monday.
Due to being understaffed all summer, the clinic cut its hours.
Errors due to rounding may cause the totals to differ slightly.

entries.ipa: /ˈnɛkst ˈdɔr tu/ · casual /ˈnɛks ˈdɔr tə/ (the first t usually drops)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun (next door to us); never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative naming premises is fine (next door to what is now a nail salon). Sense 2 takes only an adjective or an abstract noun of extremity (next door to impossible, next door to a miracle).
entries.pattern: [clause] next door to [noun phrase] · be next door to [adjective / noun]
entries.contrast: Against next to, this asserts the specific relation of adjacent premises: next door to the bakery is the building beside it, where next to the bakery could be a parked car or a mailbox. Sense 2 is a fixed intensifier meaning "very nearly," and it survives only with words at the end of a scale — next door to impossible works, next door to difficult does not. Bare next door is an adverb and takes no object: They live next door, Ask next door — where the preposition always requires one.
entries.meaning: 1. In the building or unit immediately adjacent to. They live next door to the elementary school. 2. Very nearly; barely short of (informal). Getting a permit that fast is next door to impossible.
examples: They live next door to the elementary school.
The pharmacy is next door to the hardware store, not across from it.
We moved in next door to her parents and stayed nine years.
The office is next door to mine, which is how I hear everything.
Getting a permit that fast is next door to impossible.
His third album is next door to unlistenable.

entries.ipa: /ˈnɛkst tu/ · casual /ˈnɛks tə/ (the first t usually drops)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative naming a place or a thing is fine (next to what used to be the bakery). Sense 2 takes only a small set of negative quantifiers (nothing, no one, never, impossible).
entries.pattern: [clause] next to [noun phrase] · Next to [noun phrase], [clause]. · next to [negative quantifier]
entries.contrast: Against beside, which means the same thing and is one word shorter, next to is the more common in American speech. Do not confuse beside with besides: beside is the spatial word, "at the side of," while besides means "in addition to" or "apart from" (Besides the rent, there's insurance). The fixed idiom is beside the point, meaning irrelevant — and besides the point is simply an error for it, not a phrase with a meaning of its own. Against close to, next to requires immediate adjacency — nothing between the two things. Sense 2, next to nothing, is a fixed idiom meaning "almost none" and has no spatial content; sense 3 is comparative and means "compared with." Bare next is a determiner or an adverb and takes no object — next week, Who's next?, the house next door — where the preposition always has one.
entries.meaning: 1. Immediately beside. She sat next to the window. 2. Almost (with a negative). He knows next to nothing about cars. 3. Compared with. Next to last year's model, this one feels cheap.
examples: She sat next to the window the whole flight.
The pharmacy is next to the hardware store.
Put the recycling bin next to the garage, not in front of it.
He knows next to nothing about cars.
The repair cost next to nothing.
Next to last year's model, this one feels cheap.
Next to her, everyone else on the panel looked unprepared.

entries.type: complex (adjective + fixed preposition; marginal — it is closer to an adjective governing its complement than to a true unit)
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund — and, the to being a preposition, never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: be obedient to [noun phrase] · [noun] obedient to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Listed here because it patterns like contrary to and pursuant to, but it is the weakest member of the family: obedient is a fully live adjective and to is simply the preposition it takes, so the two do not fuse the way according to does. Compare subject to, which has fused much further and has developed meanings the adjective subject no longer carries on its own. In modern American prose, obeys or complies with is nearly always better.
entries.meaning: Says the subject submits to an authority, a law, or a principle. It is the vocabulary of scripture, oaths, and nineteenth-century prose, and outside those settings it sounds antique.
examples: The design is obedient to the constraints of the site.
A citizen is obedient to the law, not to the officer enforcing it.
The prose is obedient to a rhythm that never varies.
He remained obedient to the vows he had taken at twenty.
Every part of the machine is obedient to a single cam.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only. The to is a preposition, so opposed to raise the fee is wrong — it must be opposed to raising the fee. Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is marginal and best avoided.
entries.pattern: be/remain opposed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · [noun] opposed to [noun phrase] · strongly/bitterly/firmly/implacably opposed to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Distinguish this sharply from as opposed to, which is a different item doing a different job: She is opposed to the plan states a position, while a grant, as opposed to a loan draws a definitional line and states no position at all. Dropping the as changes the sentence from a clarification into an assertion of belief, and the two are confused constantly. Against plain against, which is shorter and says the same thing (She is against the plan), opposed to is the formal register's choice and grades more freely. Against in favor of, it is the exact antonym and takes the same complements.
entries.meaning: States that the subject holds a position of resistance. Because it is a participial adjective rather than a verb, it reports a settled stance rather than an act of opposing, which is why committees and editorial pages reach for it.
examples: Two members are firmly opposed to the merger.
She is opposed to raising the fee in an election year.
The union is not opposed to automation as such.
He remained bitterly opposed to the settlement until the last day.
Voters opposed to the measure outnumbered its supporters two to one.
They are opposed to being surveyed at all.
Nobody on the board is opposed to the idea in principle.

entries.register: formal; chiefly British in the spatial sense
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause in the abstract sense (opposite to what the designers intended). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun/clause] opposite to [noun phrase / wh-clause]
entries.contrast: Bare opposite is itself a preposition and needs no to; adding to is a British habit in the spatial sense and is redundant in American prose. Against in front of, opposite requires the two things to face each other across a space. Against contrary to, which asserts conflict, opposite to asserts inversion.
variants: In American English the ordinary spatial word is bare opposite (the house opposite ours) or, far more often, across from (the house across from ours). Opposite to survives in American usage mainly in the abstract sense "the reverse of."
entries.meaning: Places one thing facing or inverting another. American writers should prefer across from for places and the opposite of for abstractions.
examples: The effect was exactly opposite to what the designers intended.
Their conclusions are opposite to ours in every particular.
The pharmacy sits opposite to the courthouse. (chiefly British; American: across from)
Warm air moves opposite to the surface current.
Her instinct runs opposite to his on almost every question.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (owing to what the survey found). Never a that-clause — owing to the fact that is the clause-taking workaround. The to is a preposition, so never a bare infinitive: owing to being closed, not owing to be closed.
entries.pattern: Owing to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] owing to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Owing to is the preposition that traditionalists prescribe instead of adverbial due to: Owing to fog, the flight was canceled has never been disputed, while Due to fog, ... has. The two are otherwise synonymous, and both mean because of. In American English owing to is noticeably more formal and less frequent than in British English.
entries.meaning: Names the cause of the situation in the main clause. Its safety in the sentence-adverbial position is its whole reason for surviving alongside because of.
examples: Owing to a scheduling conflict, the hearing was moved to Thursday.
The shortfall is owing to lower-than-expected enrollment.
Owing to the drought, the district imposed watering restrictions.
Several flights were delayed owing to a systems failure at the tower.
Owing to being closed for renovation, the branch is not accepting returns.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (prior to signing). Never a bare infinitive — prior to sign the lease is wrong — and never a that-clause or a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] prior to [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · Prior to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Prior to means before, and before is almost always better. It is the most reliably flagged padding in this whole family; usage guides from Fowler onward have called it a needless formality. Keep it only where before would be ambiguous with the spatial sense, or in legal drafting where it is conventional. Note that prior alone is an adjective (a prior conviction), not a preposition.
entries.meaning: Places an event earlier than another. Its one real advantage over before is that it cannot be misread as spatial.
examples: All applications must be received prior to the March 1 deadline.
Prior to signing, read the arbitration clause carefully.
She had no experience in the field prior to 2019.
Employees hired prior to the merger keep their original benefits.
Prior to the storm, the reservoir was already at capacity.

entries.register: legal — essentially confined to statutes, contracts, and court filings
entries.complement: noun phrase only, almost always a legal instrument. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund, and never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] pursuant to [noun phrase]. · Pursuant to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Means "under, in accordance with, as authorized by." Against in accordance with, it is narrower — the object must be a rule or authority that empowers the action, not merely a standard the action matched. Plain-language drafting guides recommend under in nearly every case: under Section 12 says what pursuant to Section 12 says.
entries.meaning: Grounds an action in the legal authority that permits it. It is one of the few prepositions in English whose register is essentially a single profession.
examples: The subpoena was issued pursuant to Rule 45.
Pursuant to the settlement agreement, the payments begin in January.
Records are released pursuant to a valid public-records request.
The officer conducted the search pursuant to a warrant.
Pursuant to state law, the notice must run for three consecutive weeks.

entries.register: formal; technical in sense 1, bureaucratic in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (relative to what we paid last year). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] relative to [noun phrase] · Relative to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is quantitative and is the standard scientific and financial word for a benchmark comparison. Sense 2 means "concerning" and is stiff bureaucratic English for about — the same criticism that applies to in terms of and with regard to. Against compared with, sense 1 implies a proportional or normalized comparison, not just a side-by-side one.
entries.meaning: 1. In comparison with; measured against. Wages have fallen relative to housing costs. 2. Concerning; with regard to. The memo raises questions relative to the timeline.
examples: Wages have fallen sharply relative to housing costs.
The fund underperformed relative to its benchmark for the third year running.
Motion is only meaningful relative to a chosen frame of reference.
The city's crime rate is low relative to comparable metros.
The memo raises several questions relative to the proposed timeline.
Please forward any documents relative to the 2023 audit.

entries.respell: SIM-uh-lur too — not /ˈsɪmjələr/; there is no y sound in it
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (similar to mine), gerund (similar to running a small business), or a free relative (similar to what we saw last year). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: similar to filing, not similar to file.
entries.pattern: [X] is similar to [Y] · very / broadly / roughly / strikingly similar to [noun phrase] · [noun] similar to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Similar to takes to; different from takes from — two exact opposites with opposite prepositions, and both similar with and similar than are errors. Against like, the one-word preposition doing the same job (a car like mine), similar to is the written, hedged form and grades freely in a way like cannot: broadly similar to has no like equivalent. Against the same as, it deliberately stops short of identity — things similar to each other are not claimed to match.
entries.meaning: Asserts resemblance without asserting identity. Because it is gradable, the real information is usually in the adverb in front of it rather than in the phrase itself.
examples: The new policy is similar to one Ohio adopted in 2019.
Her handwriting is strikingly similar to her mother's.
Running a clinic is similar to running a small business, only with worse hours.
The symptoms are broadly similar to what we saw last winter.
This one is similar to mine but a generation older.
The two proposals are similar to each other in everything but price.

entries.respell: SUB-jikt too — adjective stress on the first syllable; the verb subject is /səbˈdʒɛkt/, sub-JEKT
entries.register: neutral to formal; sense 3 is the language of contracts and offers
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. The to is a preposition, so subject to be approved is wrong — write subject to being approved, or better, the nominal subject to approval. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: be subject to [noun phrase] · [noun phrase], subject to [noun phrase] · subject to change / approval / availability / audit (fixed collocations)
entries.contrast: Three senses a reader must keep apart, because only the third makes the surrounding statement provisional: The offer is final, subject to board approval is not a final offer, and the whole force of the sentence sits in those three words. Sense 1 is liability, sense 2 is disposition, sense 3 is conditionality. Watch the stress and the part of speech — subjected to is the passive verb and means "made to undergo" (subjected to questioning), which is not this item. Against obedient to, which never fused, subject to has developed meanings the adjective subject no longer carries alone; against pursuant to, it names a condition rather than an authorizing rule.
entries.meaning: 1. Liable to; exposed to (a charge, penalty, or requirement). Late filings are subject to a fifty-dollar penalty. 2. Prone to; repeatedly affected by. The valley is subject to flash flooding. 3. Conditional on; not final until (contract language). The sale is subject to financing.
examples: Late filings are subject to a fifty-dollar penalty.
All imports are subject to inspection at the port of entry.
Contractors are subject to the same conduct code as employees.
The valley is subject to flash flooding every spring.
He has been subject to migraines since his twenties.
Prices are subject to change without notice.
The sale is subject to financing and a clean inspection.
The appointment is subject to being confirmed by the full council.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a bare infinitive — subsequent to filing, not subsequent to file.
entries.pattern: [clause] subsequent to [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · Subsequent to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: The mirror image of prior to, and subject to the same criticism: after is shorter and clearer in nearly every sentence. It is genuinely useful only in accounting and legal contexts where subsequent events is a term of art. Note that subsequent alone is an adjective and takes no complement.
entries.meaning: Places an event later than another. Like prior to, its persistence owes more to the gravity of official registers than to any distinction it draws.
examples: Subsequent to the merger, three regional offices were closed.
No changes were made subsequent to the final review.
Claims filed subsequent to the deadline will not be considered.
Subsequent to filing the report, the auditor discovered a second error.
The property was rezoned subsequent to the 2019 general plan update.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (thanks to being warned early), or a nominal wh-clause (thanks to what the neighbors did). Never a that-clause — the workaround is because.
entries.pattern: Thanks to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] thanks to [noun phrase]. · no thanks to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: A causal preposition that normally credits a welcome cause, which is what separates it from neutral because of. Its ironic use — Thanks to you, we missed the exit — is extremely common and depends entirely on tone; the fixed no thanks to (We finished on time, no thanks to him) makes the blame explicit. Do not confuse with the plural noun in give thanks to or with the greeting thanks to everyone who came, where thanks is a noun and to marks its recipient — the test is whether the sentence has a separate outcome being explained.
entries.meaning: Attributes an outcome to a person or factor, with an evaluative charge that plain because of lacks. Read the surrounding sentence to know whether the charge is gratitude or sarcasm. 1. Because of (a welcome cause); with credit to. Thanks to a last-minute donation, the shelter stayed open. 2. Because of (an unwelcome cause) — ironic, and equally common. Thanks to you, we missed the exit. 3. no thanks to — despite the failure of (fixed). We finished on time, no thanks to the detour signs.
examples: Thanks to a last-minute donation, the shelter stayed open.
She finished the degree in three years thanks to summer courses.
The team is in the playoffs thanks to a kicker nobody had heard of in August.
Thanks to being warned a day early, we moved the equipment in time.
Thanks to you, we missed the exit and drove twenty miles the wrong way.
Thanks to one clause nobody read, the lease renews automatically.
We got there on time, no thanks to the detour signs.
The roof held, no thanks to the contractor who installed it.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund in sense 5 (up to running a marathon), or a nominal wh-clause in sense 6 (up to whoever signs off on it). Never a that-clause. In sense 4 the complement is nearly always a vague or negative noun (something, no good, what). Note that sense 6 also licenses a following to-infinitive on a separate subject — It's up to the board to decide — which is a different slot, not this preposition's complement.
entries.pattern: up to [quantity] · [verb of motion] up to [place] · be up to [noun phrase] · It's up to [person] to [verb] · be up to [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Up alone is an adverb or a particle (Stand up, Look it up); up to is the preposition and always has an object. Sense 1's "maximum" reading is a persistent source of advertising complaints: save up to 50% guarantees nothing, because it names a ceiling, not a floor. Sense 2 is the plain spatial one and is the sense the others are built out of — a limit reached and not passed. Sense 6, it's up to you, is one of the most frequent uses in speech and is invisible to learners who only know sense 1.
entries.meaning: 1. As many or as much as; not exceeding (a ceiling). The theater holds up to four hundred people. 2. As far as; right up to (a point reached in space). She walked up to the counter and asked for a refund. 3. Until (a point in time). Everything was fine up to the last week of rehearsals. 4. Engaged in (usually something suspect). What are those two up to? 5. Capable of; equal to. He isn't up to the job. 6. The responsibility or choice of. It's up to the board now.
examples: The theater holds up to four hundred people.
Fines run up to five thousand dollars per violation.
She walked up to the counter and asked for a refund.
The water came up to my knees before I turned back.
Everything went smoothly up to the last week of rehearsals.
Up to that point, she had never missed a shift.
What are those two up to in the garage?
He's been up to no good since he got here.
She wasn't up to a five-mile hike two months after surgery.
Nobody thought the rookie would be up to the pressure.
It's up to the board now, not to me.
Whether we go at all is up to the weather.

entries.ipa: /æz ə rɪˈzʌlt əv/ · weak /əz ə rɪˈzʌlt əv/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (as a result of being understaffed), or a nominal wh-clause (as a result of what the audit turned up). Never a that-clause — the clause-taking form is as a result of the fact that, which is worth avoiding, or simply because.
entries.pattern: [clause] as a result of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · As a result of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: The bare adverbial as a result is not this preposition. With no complement it is a conjunctive adverb joining two sentences: Sales fell. As a result, we cut hours. The preposition requires an object. Against because of, this is heavier and frames the object as a cause whose consequences are being traced; against due to, it is adverbial and therefore never disputed.
entries.meaning: Names the event or condition whose consequence the main clause reports. It is the causal preposition of reports and investigations, where the point is usually to establish a chain rather than simply assign a reason.
examples: Two hundred jobs were lost as a result of the merger.
As a result of the audit, three policies were rewritten.
She missed a month of school as a result of the surgery.
Premiums rose sharply as a result of last year's claims.
As a result of being understaffed, the clinic cut its weekend hours.
The bridge was closed as a result of damage found during a routine inspection.

entries.complement: Three different grammars. As a preposition of distance it takes a noun phrase naming a place or point (as far as Denver). As a topic marker it takes a noun phrase that must be closed by is concerned, goes, or a similar verb — as far as the budget is concerned. As a conjunction it takes a full finite clause (as far as I know). It never takes a gerund.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] as far as [place] · As far as [noun phrase] is concerned, [clause]. · as far as [clause] (conjunction)
entries.contrast: The truncation trap. In speech Americans routinely drop the completing verb — As far as money, we're fine — and editors routinely restore it. The phrase that needs no verb is as for: As for money, we're fine is correct as it stands. The two are one syllable apart and are constantly swapped. The distance sense is treated with the movement prepositions and the full topic formula with the topic prepositions; both are linked below.
entries.meaning: 1. To the point of; up to (distance). We drove as far as Santa Fe and turned around. 2. To the extent or limit of (degree). The offer goes as far as free replacement, but no further. 3. On the subject of (topic; requires is concerned or goes). As far as the schedule is concerned, nothing has changed.
examples: We drove as far as Santa Fe and then turned around.
The trail runs as far as the second ridge.
Fires were reported as far as forty miles from the coast.
The company will go as far as a partial refund and no further.
