As far as the schedule is concerned, nothing has changed.
As far as the money goes, we're covered through March.
As far as I know, the meeting is still on.
related: as far as X is concerned

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (as for me, never as for I), gerund (as for finding a replacement), or a nominal wh-clause (as for what happens next). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: As for [noun phrase], [clause]. — overwhelmingly sentence-initial; the postposed [clause] as for [noun phrase] is unidiomatic.
entries.contrast: As for needs no completing verb, where as far as does: As for the budget, we're fine / As far as the budget is concerned, we're fine. Against as to, which introduces an uncertainty or a question, as for introduces a contrasting participant that has already been mentioned — it presupposes prior context and cannot open a conversation cold. Against regarding, it is conversational rather than bureaucratic.
entries.meaning: Shifts the topic to one item already in play, usually to say something different about it from what was just said about the others. The characteristic rhythm is a list followed by an exception: everyone else did X; as for him, he did Y.
examples: As for me, I'd rather stay home.
The others left at six. As for Dana, nobody knows.
As for the money, we'll figure that out later.
As for your second question, I don't have an answer yet.
As for finding a replacement, the search starts Monday.
He's furious. As for the rest of us, we're just tired.

entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in business, legal, and news writing
entries.complement: a time expression only — a date, a clock time, or a temporal noun (as of Monday, as of noon, as of today, as of this writing). Never a clause of any kind, never a gerund, and never a non-temporal noun: as of the merger is wrong unless the merger is being treated as a dated event.
entries.pattern: As of [time], [clause]. · [clause] as of [time].
entries.contrast: Two readings, and the tense of the main verb decides which. A present or future verb gives "starting from": As of Monday, the rate goes up. A past or perfect verb gives "at the point of, and up to": As of Friday, no one had called. Against plain from, as of fixes an official effective moment rather than a starting edge; against by, it names a snapshot rather than a deadline. British as from is rare in American English.
entries.meaning: 1. Starting from; with effect from (a future or announced point). As of January 1, the fee increases. 2. At the moment of; up to and including (a snapshot of a state). As of last night, forty units were still unsold.
examples: As of January 1, the parking fee increases to twelve dollars.
The new policy takes effect as of Monday morning.
She is, as of this week, the longest-serving member of the board.
As of Friday, no one had returned the call.
As of last night, forty units were still unsold.
The balance as of the close of business was $4,318.
As of this writing, the vote count has not been certified.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (as opposed to waiting), or a nominal wh-clause (as opposed to what most people assume). Never a that-clause and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: as opposed to wait is wrong. The complement must be grammatically parallel to the item it corrects.
entries.pattern: [X] as opposed to [Y] · [clause], as opposed to [noun phrase / verb-ing].
entries.contrast: It does not merely contrast, it corrects — it names the thing that is not the case, usually because a reader might have assumed it was. Against instead of, which reports a substitution that actually took place (We took the train instead of driving), as opposed to draws a definitional line (a commuter train, as opposed to a freight line). Against rather than, it is heavier and more explicitly clarifying; against unlike, it does not compare qualities.
entries.meaning: Marks the alternative that is being ruled out. Because its job is to head off a misreading, it is at its most useful when the two options are genuinely confusable.
examples: This is a recommendation, as opposed to an order.
She works in public health, as opposed to clinical medicine.
We're talking about the 1980 election, as opposed to the primary.
The grant funds research, as opposed to construction.
He chose to negotiate, as opposed to walking away.
The figure is annual, as opposed to monthly.

entries.register: commercial and bureaucratic; widely disliked in edited prose
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] as per [noun phrase]. · As per [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A redundancy. Latin per already means "according to," so the as adds nothing: per your request and according to your request both say what as per your request says, in fewer words. Usage guides across the board recommend per, according to, in accordance with, or following. The one form with a life of its own is the jocular fixed phrase as per usual, which nobody intends seriously.
entries.meaning: Cites an instruction, agreement, or standard as the authority for what was done. It is boilerplate — the language of purchase orders and shipping notices — and it signals institutional register more than it carries meaning.
examples: The goods were shipped as per your instructions.
Payment is due in thirty days as per the contract.
As per the attached schedule, the site closes at four.
Invoices will be processed as per company policy.
He was late again, as per usual.
The panels were installed as per the manufacturer's drawings.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (as regards what was agreed). Never a that-clause. And note what cannot follow it at all: as regards to is an error — the phrase takes no to.
entries.pattern: As regards [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] as regards [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: With regard to needs its to; as regards refuses one. The reason is grammatical history: in with regard to, regard is a noun that requires the preposition to, while in as regards the -s is the third-person verb ending of an old impersonal clause ("as [it] regards"), and a verb takes its object directly. Learners who know one form contaminate the other, producing as regards to and with regards to, both wrong.
entries.meaning: Introduces the topic of the statement. It is the most formal of the topic markers and reads as slightly archaic in American prose, where regarding, on, or about almost always fits better.
examples: As regards the second contract, negotiations are ongoing.
The report is silent as regards enforcement.
As regards staffing, the department has made no decision.
Nothing has changed as regards eligibility.
As regards funding the expansion, the board remains divided.

entries.register: formal; very heavy in legal writing
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (as to whether the signature is genuine, as to what happened next). Never a that-clause — as to that he was late is impossible.
entries.pattern: As to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [noun of uncertainty] as to [wh-clause] · [clause] as to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Two jobs with different fates. Fronted, it is a topic-shifter and a stiffer twin of as for. Mid-sentence after a noun of uncertainty — question, doubt, dispute, evidence, confusion — it introduces the content of that uncertainty, and there it is very often deletable: no question as to whether he signed is simply no question whether he signed. Against about, it is the formal register's choice and is usually padding outside legal drafting.
entries.meaning: Attaches a topic or a specification to what precedes it. Its survival in American English is almost entirely a legal phenomenon; in ordinary prose about, on, or of replaces it without loss. 1. On the subject of (fronted topic-shifter). As to the second charge, the defense concedes nothing. 2. Introducing the content of a question, doubt, or dispute. There is real doubt as to whether the signature is genuine.
examples: As to the second charge, the defense concedes nothing.
As to your fee, we can discuss it after the hearing.
There is real doubt as to whether the signature is genuine.
The parties disagree as to the meaning of Section 4.
She gave no hint as to what she would decide.
The statute is silent as to remedies.
Opinions differ sharply as to how the money should be spent.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (as well as what the grant covers). Never a that-clause. When the added item is a verb and the main clause already has a finite verb of its own, the gerund is obligatory: She runs the department as well as teaching two sections, not as well as teach. (The pattern He writes as well as directs, with two finite verbs sharing one subject, is as well as working as a coordinating conjunction, not as this preposition.)
entries.pattern: [subject], as well as [noun phrase], [singular verb] · [clause] as well as [noun phrase / verb-ing].
entries.contrast: Two traps, both common. First, verb agreement: as well as does not build a compound subject, so The manager, as well as two clerks, was present — singular, where and would give were. The same holds for along with, together with, and in addition to. Second, it is not a synonym for and: it subordinates, presenting the material after it as the lesser or already-known item, so He plays guitar as well as piano foregrounds the guitar. Distinguish also the ordinary comparative as well as meaning "as skillfully as": She sings as well as her sister is a comparison of ability, not an addition.
entries.meaning: Adds a second item while keeping it grammatically and rhetorically subordinate to the first. That subordination is the whole point, and it is why writers who mean plain coordination should use and.
examples: The fee covers materials as well as labor.
The senator, as well as two aides, was subpoenaed.
She runs the department as well as teaching two sections a semester.
He speaks Korean as well as Japanese.
As well as the main gallery, there's a sculpture garden out back.
The storm knocked out power in three counties as well as half of the next state.
She sings as well as her sister does, which is saying something.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (along with paying the fine), or a nominal wh-clause (along with whatever else you need). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [subject], along with [noun phrase], [singular verb] · [clause] along with [noun phrase]. · Along with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Verb agreement trap, identical to as well as, together with, and in addition to: The coach, along with two players, was fined. The parenthetical material never joins the subject. Against plain with, along with stresses that the two share the action or the fate rather than merely being present together. Bare along is a different word — an adverb (Bring the kids along) or a preposition of path (a walk along the river).
entries.meaning: Adds a second participant to whatever the subject is doing or undergoing. It is the neutral, everyday member of the addition group, less formal than together with and less rhetorically loaded than as well as. 1. In the company of; accompanying. She arrived along with the rest of the delegation. 2. In addition to; at the same time as. The bill raises fees along with penalties.
examples: She arrived along with the rest of the delegation.
Send the signed form along with two forms of ID.
The coach, along with two assistants, was placed on leave.
Three warehouses burned, along with everything inside them.
Along with paying the fine, he lost his license for a year.
Her name appeared on the list along with forty others.

entries.ipa: /æt ˈɑdz wɪθ/ · weak /ət ˈɑdz wəθ/ — at reduces to /ət/
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative (at odds with what the data show). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be at odds with [noun phrase] · [noun] at odds with [noun phrase] · sharply/fundamentally/wildly at odds with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The negative counterpart of in keeping with and in line with: those report that two things fit, this reports that they do not. It stops well short of in violation of — being at odds with something alleges inconsistency, not breach — which is why it is the safe word for a claim that clashes with the evidence rather than with a rule. With a person as the object it means an ongoing quarrel (at odds with her own caucus), and there both sides are animate and the relation is mutual. Bare at odds, with no complement, is a predicate phrase and takes no object: The two of them have been at odds for years. The odds here is invariable and has nothing to do with betting.
entries.meaning: Reports that two things are inconsistent with each other. The subject and the complement are treated as equals, which is why the phrase can be reversed without changing what it claims.
examples: His account is sharply at odds with the security footage.
The policy is at odds with everything the mayor campaigned on.
She has been at odds with her own caucus since January.
The findings are at odds with three earlier studies.
The new wing is wildly at odds with the rest of the block.
Their numbers are at odds with what the state reported for the same month.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause and never a wh-clause — the clause equivalent is the conjunction if it had not been for the fact that, or simply if ... had not.
entries.pattern: But for [noun phrase], [main clause with would, would have, or could have]. — the counterfactual verb is not optional.
entries.contrast: It requires a conditional main clause. But for means "if it had not been for," so the sentence must state what would otherwise have happened: But for the delay, we would have made the connection. A plain indicative after it (But for the delay, we missed the connection) is wrong. Against except for, which subtracts a real exception from a real situation, but for names a cause that did operate and asks the reader to imagine it away. The but here is the old preposition meaning "except," not the conjunction.
entries.meaning: Introduces the one thing whose absence would have changed the outcome. Legal writing has made it a term of art: the but-for test asks whether the injury would have occurred without the defendant's act.
examples: But for the seatbelt, she would not have survived.
But for a last-minute donation, the shelter would have closed.
But for his testimony, the case would never have gone to trial.
The building would be gone but for a single preservation lawsuit.
But for the weather, we would have finished the roof on Tuesday.
But for one dissenting vote, the measure would have passed unanimously.

entries.complement: noun phrase or a nominal wh-clause — depending on what you order, depending on whether it rains, depending on how far you drive. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause], depending on [noun phrase / wh-clause]. · Depending on [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: It has frozen completely: it needs no subject and cannot dangle, unlike the live participle in Depending on his brother for rides, he never bought a car, where depending still belongs to he. Against according to, which reports what a source says, depending on names a variable that determines the outcome. Its free acceptance of wh-clauses puts it in a very small group with regardless of, irrespective of, and as to.
variants: depending upon is the formal variant and means exactly the same thing.
entries.meaning: Makes the main clause conditional on a factor that may vary. It is the standard way English states a range of outcomes without writing a conditional sentence.
examples: The trip takes two or three hours, depending on traffic.
Depending on the weather, the ceremony will be inside or out.
Fees range from $40 to $120 depending on the size of the lot.
Depending on what the inspector finds, we may have to start over.
She'll fly or drive, depending on whether the fare drops.
Turnout could double or halve depending on how the case is decided.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (except for me), gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (except for what he told the police). Never a that-clause — the clause form is the conjunction except that (The house is perfect except that it has no garage).
entries.pattern: Except for [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] except for [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Except for versus bare except. Use except for when the exception is fronted (Except for Tuesday, I'm free) and when it subtracts from a whole rather than from a matching list item; use bare except when the exception is parallel to something explicit in the sentence (Everyone came except Dave). Against apart from and aside from, which can also mean "in addition to," except for only subtracts — which makes it the right choice whenever the exception reading must be unmistakable.
entries.meaning: 1. Apart from; with the exception of. Except for two typos, the manuscript is clean. 2. If it were not for (a factor that prevented something). Except for the rain, we would have finished the roof.
examples: Except for two typos, the manuscript is clean.
The office is empty except for the night guard.
I like everything on the menu except for the oysters.
Except for Tuesday, I'm free all week.
Except for the rain, we would have finished the roof.
The team would be in first place except for a bad October.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (for fear of waking the baby). Never a that-clause — the clause-taking companion is the conjunction for fear that (for fear that the baby would wake), which is a different item, exactly as in case is to in case of. A free relative is fine, since it is a noun phrase (for fear of what the neighbors would say), and never an infinitive: for fear of to wake the baby is wrong.
entries.pattern: [negative or cautious clause] for fear of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · [clause] for fear that [clause] — the conjunction, not this preposition.
entries.contrast: It gives the feared outcome as the reason something was not done, so the main clause is characteristically negative, hedged, or evasive — said nothing, never reported it, kept the door locked. Against because of, the feared thing need never have happened at all, which is exactly the difference between a cause and a motive. Against to avoid, which takes the same gerund and names the same purpose, for fear of adds the emotion and concedes the timidity. Its structural neighbor is for lack of, which blames an absence where this one blames an anticipation.
variants: out of fear of is the looser, more psychological variant. Do not confuse it with in fear of, which means "afraid of" and names a state rather than a motive: living in fear of deportation is how someone feels, he said nothing for fear of deportation is why he acted.
entries.meaning: Names the outcome whose prospect stopped the subject from acting. The phrase reports a motive rather than a cause, and the motive is always avoidance.
examples: She said nothing for fear of making it worse.
Nobody reported the leak for fear of losing the contract.
Witnesses would not come forward for fear of retaliation.
They moved the horses inside for fear of the storm.
He avoided the subject entirely for fear of another argument.
The family kept the diagnosis quiet for fear of what the neighbors would say.

entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a bare abstract or mass noun (for lack of evidence, for lack of funding). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] for lack of [noun phrase]. · for lack of anything better · for lack of a better [noun]
entries.contrast: It states a cause that consists in an absence, which is exactly what separates it from because of: dismissed because of the evidence and dismissed for lack of evidence say opposite things. Against in the absence of, which supplies a condition and looks forward (in the absence of an agreement, state law governs), for lack of supplies a reason and looks back at something that has already failed. The apologetic formula for lack of a better word is fixed and cannot be varied.
variants: For want of is the older and more literary twin — For want of a nail the shoe was lost — and is somewhat commoner in British English
for lack of is the ordinary American form. Both take the same complement, and neither puts an article on the noun unless the noun demands one.
entries.meaning: Gives the missing thing as the reason for the outcome, and the outcome is nearly always a failure, a refusal, or a collapse. Because the phrase blames an absence, it cannot take an object that was present.
examples: The case was dismissed for lack of evidence.
The project died for lack of funding.
For lack of a better word, the meeting was a disaster.
Two positions went unfilled for lack of qualified applicants.
The garden failed for lack of water, not for lack of attention.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ðə ˈpɜrpəs əv/ · weak /fər ðə ˈpɜrpə sə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only (for the purpose of raising revenue). Because of is a preposition, for the purpose of to raise revenue is wrong, and so is for the purpose to raise revenue. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] for the purpose of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · For the purposes of [this section], [definition].
entries.contrast: Against the plain infinitive of purpose, which says the same thing in two words, this is nearly always padding: for the purpose of reducing costs is to reduce costs. Keep it where the purpose has to appear as a formal element — tax law, permits, definitions — and cut it everywhere else. Against with a view to, which takes the same gerund but implies the goal has not been reached, for the purpose of simply names the aim; against for the sake of, which names a beneficiary or a value, this names an objective.
variants: The plural for the purposes of is the standard opening of a definition clause — For the purposes of this Act, "employee" means… — and is not interchangeable with the singular, which states an aim rather than a scope.
entries.meaning: States the aim an action was designed to serve. Its survival is entirely institutional: it marks the purpose as officially declared rather than merely intended.
examples: The land was acquired for the purpose of building a transfer station.
The account exists for the purpose of holding client funds and nothing else.
For the purposes of this section, "resident" means a person domiciled in the state.
Records may be retained for the purpose of audit.
He formed the company for the purpose of limiting his personal liability.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ðə ˈseɪk əv/ · weak /fər ðə ˈseɪk əv/ · casual /fər ðə ˈseɪ kə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (for the sake of keeping the peace). Never a that-clause; a free relative is possible but uncommon (for the sake of whoever comes after us).
entries.pattern: [clause] for the sake of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · For the sake of [noun phrase], [clause]. · for [possessive] sake (fixed: for heaven's sake)
entries.contrast: The two senses below are told apart by whether the object is animate. Against on behalf of, which means "as the agent of," this means "for the benefit of," and confusing them makes a speaker claim authority they do not have. The possessive forms — for heaven's sake, for old times' sake, for goodness' sake — are a separate frozen construction and take no of.
variants: for the sake of argument and the possessive pattern for argument's sake are both current
the possessive drops both the and of.
entries.meaning: Names the person served or the end pursued. The purpose reading is the commoner one in writing, where it introduces a stylistic or argumentative goal rather than a beneficiary. 1. For the benefit of (a person or group). They stayed together for the sake of the children. 2. In order to achieve or preserve (a purpose or quality). For the sake of clarity, let me restate the question.
examples: They stayed together for the sake of the children.
She took the fall for the sake of the team.
He gave up the appeal for the sake of his mother, who could not face another hearing.
For the sake of clarity, let me restate the question.
He conceded the point for the sake of argument.
For the sake of keeping the peace, nobody mentioned the will.
Don't argue for the sake of arguing.

entries.register: formal correspondence; markedly more British than American
entries.complement: noun phrase only — a document, a message, or a prior exchange. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund, and never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: Further to [noun phrase], [clause]. — almost always the opening words of a letter or an email.
entries.contrast: A letter-opening formula meaning "following up on." In American business writing it reads as imported; following up on, regarding, or plain about is the native equivalent. Against with reference to, which points at a document as a source, further to points at a prior exchange and promises to continue it. Do not confuse with the comparative adverb further (We went further than planned), which takes no object.
entries.meaning: Links the present message to an earlier one. It is nearly pure register: it carries no meaning that the reader would miss if the phrase were cut.
examples: Further to your email of March 3, the position remains open.
Further to our conversation, I've attached the revised figures.
Further to the committee's request, the data is enclosed.
Further to my previous letter, the deadline has been extended.
Further to the notice of April 12, no further action is required.

entries.complement: unusually wide — a noun phrase, an objective-case pronoun (other than her), a gerund, an adverb (other than briefly), a whole prepositional phrase (other than by mail), or a nominal wh-clause (nothing other than what he said). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [negative or universal clause] other than [complement] · Other than [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: It is most idiomatic after a negative or a universal — nothing other than, anyone other than, no way other than. After a plain positive statement it sounds stiff. Against except for, it is more formal and far more willing to take adverbial complements: other than by mail is fine, except for by mail is not. Against besides, which can add a second item, other than only subtracts. Neither half is this word on its own: other is a determiner or adjective (the other door), and than by itself is the comparative — a conjunction before a clause (taller than I am) and a preposition before a pronoun (taller than me). And it is other than, never other then.
entries.meaning: 1. Apart from; besides. We have no evidence other than his statement. 2. In any way but; differently from. You cannot reach the island other than by ferry.
examples: We have no evidence other than his own statement.
Other than a sore shoulder, he came through it fine.
Nobody other than the two of us has the code.
She has never lived anywhere other than Ohio.
You cannot reach the island other than by ferry.
He has never spoken about it other than briefly, and never on the record.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (over and above meeting the minimum). Never a that-clause; a free relative is fine (over and above what the contract requires).
entries.pattern: [clause] over and above [noun phrase]. · Over and above [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A four-word in addition to with one extra claim: that what came before was already enough. Over and above her salary presents the salary as the expected part and the rest as surplus, where in addition to her salary is neutral about sufficiency. Against besides, it is heavier and more emphatic. Neither half carries the meaning alone — over and above are ordinary spatial prepositions elsewhere, and the frozen pair is not spatial at all; nor can the two words be separated. The similar-sounding above and beyond is a different fixed phrase and describes effort rather than amount.
entries.meaning: Adds something to a total that was already complete. The baseline has to be recoverable from the sentence, or the phrase has nothing to measure the surplus against.
examples: She receives a housing allowance over and above her salary.
The fee is charged over and above the standard shipping rate.
Over and above the fine, he lost his license for a year.
They asked for two more inspectors over and above what the budget allowed.
The volunteers put in three hundred hours over and above running the shelter itself.

entries.complement: the freest complement in this file. A noun phrase (rather than the bus), a gerund (rather than complaining), a bare infinitive (rather than complain), an adjective (structural rather than personal), an adverb, a prepositional phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (rather than what was proposed). Never a that-clause. After a to-infinitive it takes a bare infinitive: He chose to walk rather than wait.
entries.pattern: [X] rather than [Y] — X and Y parallel · Rather than [Y], [clause]. · [subject], rather than [noun phrase], [singular verb]
entries.contrast: The bare-infinitive privilege is what separates it from instead of, which must nominalize: rather than complain is correct, instead of complain is not. Verb agreement follows the as well as rule: The manager, rather than the clerks, is responsible. Note also that rather than is often a conjunction rather than a preposition — the test is what it joins: parallel phrases make it a preposition, full clauses make it a conjunction.
entries.meaning: 1. In preference to; instead of. We took the train rather than the bus. 2. And not; as opposed to (correcting a possible reading). The problem is structural rather than personal.
examples: We took the train rather than the bus.
Rather than complain, she rewrote the whole section herself.
He chose to negotiate rather than walk away.
The problem is structural rather than personal.
The change was gradual rather than sudden.
They fund research rather than construction.
The board, rather than the members, decides.
Rather than raising taxes, the city cut three programs.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (save for what little was left). Never a that-clause — the clause-taking form is the conjunction save that.
entries.pattern: [clause], save for [noun phrase]. · Save for [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A consciously elevated except for. In American prose it reads as a deliberate stylistic choice rather than a neutral one, and using it in ordinary business writing draws attention to itself. Against but for, which is counterfactual and demands a conditional main clause, save for simply subtracts from a real situation. Do not confuse the preposition with the verb save; the preposition never has a subject of its own.
variants: bare save (The room was empty save one chair) is older and even more literary
saving is archaic
save that is the clause-taking conjunction.
entries.meaning: Removes one item from an otherwise complete picture. Its natural home is descriptive narrative, where the exception is meant to stand out against an emptiness or a uniformity.
examples: The street was silent save for a dog barking two blocks over.
The house was untouched save for a cracked window at the back.
Save for one abstention, the vote was unanimous.
He remembered nothing of the evening save for the drive home.
Every ship in the harbor was lost, save for the two in dry dock.
Save for an hour on Sunday, she worked the entire week.

entries.complement: noun phrase (usually a list) or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause. The complement must be a genuine member of the class named before it — fruits such as apples, not fruits such as sweetness.
entries.pattern: [general noun] such as [example], [example] · [clause], such as [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Such as introduces examples; like introduces resemblances. The traditional rule reserves like for comparison and such as for exemplification: a writer like Hemingway means someone who resembles him, a writer such as Hemingway means him, offered as an instance. Speech ignores the distinction; edited prose still keeps it. Note the related split in the same pair: as a preposition like takes a noun phrase (He works like a machine), while as introduces a role (He works as a machine operator) and, as a conjunction, a full clause (Do as I say) — like I say is spoken English that edited prose still changes to as I say. Two mechanical points on such as: no comma before it when the examples restrict the class (fruits such as apples and pears), a comma when they merely illustrate; and do not end the list with etc., since such as already announces that the list is partial. Neither half stands alone: bare such is a determiner (such a mess) and bare as is a different preposition or a conjunction; only the pair is this item.
entries.meaning: Offers one or more members of a class as illustrations of it. The class must be stated first, which is why such as cannot open a sentence the way like sometimes can.
examples: Root vegetables such as carrots and parsnips keep for months.
Heavy industries such as steel and shipbuilding left the region entirely.
She avoids stimulants such as coffee and black tea.
The grant covers direct costs such as travel, equipment, and printing.

entries.register: formal to neutral; common in drafting and in formal reports
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (together with whatever documents you have). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [subject], together with [noun phrase], [singular verb] · [clause], together with [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Verb agreement trap, the same one as along with, as well as, and in addition to: the added item is parenthetical, so the verb agrees with the original subject alone — The report, together with the appendices, was filed Monday. Against along with, it is the more formal of the two and the one that appears in contracts and filings; against and, it deliberately refuses to build a compound subject. Bare together is an adverb and takes no object: We went together.
entries.meaning: Attaches supplementary material to a subject without merging the two. Its usefulness in drafting comes precisely from that refusal to merge: the primary item stays primary. 1. In the company of; accompanied by. Together with her brother, she inherited the farm. 2. In addition to (adding an item without joining it to the subject). The application, together with the filing fee, must reach the office by Friday.
examples: The application, together with the filing fee, must reach the office by Friday.
The deed was recorded together with two easements.
Together with her brother, she inherited the farm.
The report, together with all supporting exhibits, was filed Monday.
Send the transcript together with three letters of recommendation.
The principal, together with accrued interest, comes to just over $9,000.
She arrived together with two lawyers and said almost nothing.

entries.ipa: /ʌp əˈɡɛnst/ · also /ʌp əˈɡeɪnst/ · weak /əp əˈɡɛn(t)s/ — up reduces to /əp/ and the final t routinely drops
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative is idiomatic in sense 2 (up against whatever the league can put on the field). In the fixed idiom up against it the complement is the invariable pronoun it and nothing else may replace it.
entries.pattern: be up against [noun phrase] · [clause] up against [noun phrase] · be up against it (fixed)
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is not really a unit at all — it is the adverb up plus the ordinary preposition against, and you can drop the up (the ladder against the wall). Sense 2 is the frozen idiom, and there the up cannot go: We're up against a deadline is not We're against a deadline. Against facing, sense 2 always implies difficulty and usually implies an unfair contest.
entries.meaning: 1. Leaning on and touching (literal). He propped the ladder up against the gutter. 2. Confronted by, as an obstacle or an opponent. We're up against a hard deadline and a short staff. 3. up against it — in serious trouble, usually financial (fixed). They've been up against it since the mill closed.
examples: He propped the ladder up against the gutter.
She pushed the desk up against the far wall.
We're up against a hard deadline and two people short.
The defense is up against the best offense in the league.
Nobody realized what the small growers were up against.
You're up against twenty years of institutional habit.
The family has been up against it since the mill closed.
